utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Your Honour. It's case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all those people who are assisting us today. We shall have a 30- to 40-minute testimony of the witness during the examination-in-chief, and the Defence counsel will have as we said yesterday three and a half hours for its cross-examination. If we don't finish today, Colonel, you will have to come back tomorrow morning, but the Defence counsel might not need all this time. Much will depend on the Defence of Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to ask in view of the examination-in-chief yesterday and the part about the military police that took a long time, that the Defence of Mr. Coric be given more than the half hour envisaged if possible at all, because yesterday's examination-in-chief dedicated more than 50 per cent of the time precisely to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are quite right. The question of the military police and the meeting with Mr. Praljak perhaps, but I think the Prosecution is going to address this issue. Of course, the other Defence counsel can give up some of their time, because they are less concerned about this issue than you are. So you have the floor now, the Prosecution, for 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It falls from your witness statement that you had a number of meetings with Slobodan Praljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did you see him first? Do you remember -- I'm not talking about the date, at least about the month.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it's in the month of July. End of July, into August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances of your first meeting with Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the time that I was in -- in my area of responsibility, I had not met him initially for the first couple of months, realising that I was dealing with the OZ commander in that location on -- on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But did you have knowledge that Mr. Praljak was already present in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard that, and the reasons I say that is because on occasion meetings would be cancelled with Siljeg who was the OZ commander, and he would not be available because he was talking or apparently talking to his -- to a higher commander. And I was under the impression at that time that I began to know of his name as time proceeded -- with my time in that mission area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Siljeg in your testimony today. What was Siljeg's position?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, he was -- his headquarters was in Prozor, and he was the OZ commander, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which OZ, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Prozor area, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's go down to your first meeting. Was it an official meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one thing that stood out for me was that it was not an official meeting. I believe we met for the very first time over coffee in a town square, and I believe it was Prozor, and we were -- I had met him for the very first time, and I remember his -- the deputy or Siljeg himself or -- or whatever had been injured, and what stood out, he had been hit in the foot or shot in the foot, and the comment that was made, we were talking with each other, and the individual came over and we made comments about, you know, what had happened to him, and the story came out that he'd been shot the night before or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of conversation did you have with Mr. Praljak? Who else was present at this unofficial meeting, let's say? If you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not remember. I just remember my -- my initial contact and that being of a friendly nature. And in fact, if I remember correctly the -- I projected that in a report, that I had met him and at that point in time had made some comment as to his demeanour and what sort of individual he was and, more importantly, how he had, I would say, come forward into the situation and had taken on responsibility for the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know at the time what position was -- he was holding?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was -- once again, if I was in the mode of information or intelligence gathering I would have paid attention to that sort of detail and would have probably recorded it as such. On the day I probably began to understand that he was in fact the -- the commander above Siljeg in the area. But I can't comment and tell you exactly was he this specific, you know, division, brigade, corps, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any official meetings with Mr. Praljak afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to do once again a memory check here, and I would suggest that there was one other -- one other time that I can remember, and I believe Siljeg and himself were present, and we met in the warehouse and one of the offices, and we were talking about some -- once again, unfortunately I'd only be trying to search my memory without direct reference to reports on a specific day that would indicate that I was there and certain information was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how Mr. Praljak introduced himself to you.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what stood -- stood out in my initial contact was his demeanour being the individual that was in charge. His presence was -- was well known, and I got the impression that there was no doubt as to who was in charge and that he was there for a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you introduce yourself as one of the representatives of ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that's the only way I would introduce myself as an individual, because I wore a specific identification which was the 12 stars in those days, with -- 12 gold stars with a blue background, as well as wearing an identification badge and wearing all white. So it was very easy to see who I was and what I represented in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you take part in any official negotiations with Mr. Praljak participation in which some other people were involved?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer has to be yes, there was. Now, from -- once again, for me to recollect the exact circumstances and to what reasons, I would find it difficult to recollect without direct reference to date and time that are once again indicated in my reports. I have no doubt that there are meetings and that these meetings are conducted in the presence of himself and other commanders, and in my opinion there was no doubt who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you're talking about different commanders, was Mr. Siljeg also present --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: -- at the negotiations? And who was chairing the negotiations? I mean on the side of HVO and on your side.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be chairing if I was there by myself. If UNPROFOR was there, then it would be a joint and it would be the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was there from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be Major Graham Binns again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, now we should move into private session because we'll have to deal with a document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, the Prosecution has informed the Trial Chamber that it has finished its examination-in-chief. I shall therefore give the floor to Mr. Kovacic, who will start his cross-examination, and then Mr. Praljak will put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. I represent General Praljak here present, and first I will put some questions to you, after which General Praljak will ask you some questions himself. You described your arrival in Bosnia and the preparations you had been through, and we have had approximately the same thing from other witnesses. Let me ask you this: While you were in V2 in Gornji Vakuf, the director of the regional centre Zenica was Jean-Pierre Thebault. That is what you confirmed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Christopher Beese, in May and June, was his -- was the deputy, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recollect that, but if it is in the documents, then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber has seen enough evidence about when exactly Christopher Beese was there and the rest you confirmed. You said that on the 29th of May, you set out by car from Zenica towards Gornji Vakuf and that was your first journey in the area where you were going to spend another three months, and according to your statement from 9th October, 2001, you were accompanied by Philip Watkins, Major Skat-Rordam, and the driver Jens. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note the statement was of the 9th October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was your first day in that area when you set out from Zenica to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am confused. The dates that are coming across here are -- indicate the 9th of October, 2001. I was nowhere near this. Maybe I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's an error on the record. I am constantly talking about the 29th of May, 1993, but that's an error in the transcript. [In English] 29 May, 1993, it is your first day on the site. You're travelling from Zenica to Gornji Vakuf with the mentioned colleagues; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th of May, 1993, yes, I travelled from the area of Split up into -- past Gornji Vakuf into Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And in the course of that journey your colleagues, whom you mentioned, started briefing you on the current situation on the ground. It was your first day, and you were starting to learn about the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my first day in that specific area. I had been with the mission already three months in another area. This -- this was very specific briefings, and once again, remember, I did not go to Gornji Vakuf directly and stay there. I went back up first to Zenica, got background information there, and then moved forward or back into Gornji Vakuf and which I then undertook the responsibility for Gornji Vakuf. And of course Philip Watkins then moved on and Skat-Rordam who had been there already, if I remember correctly, at least one month, we teamed up together from that point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, I will appreciate it if you give me brief answers to my questions, and I will try to phrase them in a way that you are able to answer with yes, no, or I don't know, and -- because our time is limited, and if you give me extensive answers, I will not manage. Thank you for this information. You told my about your preparations. And you also had preparations in Zagreb on the 1st of March, 1993, in the headquarters of ECMM, and you spent five days there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb, you also underwent training, if I'm not mistaken. According to my information, training to handle Capsat equipment, also first aid refreshment training and some other skills, and, most importantly, you had a general briefing about the situation in the area where you were headed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I correct the last statement. In general briefing, it is -- it was an operational briefing which basically told you the whole situation of the whole area, realising that as we arrived individuals were placed in different locations and then got into more specific briefings on their exact location which were being put to or placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will show you one document to refresh your memory, because I don't think your recollection is correct. In -- it was in Zenica that you received training about personalities and details. In Zagreb you had a general kind of training. But let me put a document to you to refresh your memory. [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... put document on ELMO. Your Honour, I apologise, I don't have the document in e-court because I found it yesterday. [Interpretation] This document, to inform others in the courtroom, was Exhibit D76/1 from the case Prosecution versus Kordic and Cerkez. It was originally received from ECMM back then, and it was exhibited in that case. Witness -- in fact, I don't think it is under seal, but we should check to avoid all possible mistakes. I don't think it's under seal, but I'm never sure with these things. Let us assume it is not. Witness, if you've had time to leaf through it, especially pages 2, 3. The document has 7 pages. It has an introductory part, and it is divided into sections according to republics. The first part is about Croatia and the situation in Croatia, pages 1 to 4. And then on page 4 -- would the usher please turn to page 4. On page 4 begins the part about Bosnia and Herzegovina, which actually covers three important sections. We see above paragraph 21 the sub-heading "Bosnia-Herzegovina." There are three subheadings. We see the first one, "The Bosnian Serb army," VRS or BSA as we call it. Then on the following page we see the section about HVO and another one about the BH army. Now, having seen this, do you agree that this was the general briefing about the situation you received in Zagreb before going to Bosnia and Herzegovina, or even before going to your post that preceded Bosnia and Herzegovina? Bulgaria, I think it was. Can you confirm that? Was that the briefing you received?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I -- if I remember correctly, I did arrive in the ECMM in the March time frame. It was the 1st or 3rd of March. The document I see is in fact dated the 25th of February. I mean, once again to tell you that this was the briefing, I can't say that. I mean, realising the situation changed daily, and as individuals came into -- into the mission area, yes, they were brought up to speed on -- on the overall situation, but to say specifically this is the document or the briefing, I can't give you that right now. And by the time that I moved from Bulgaria to Macedonia and then back into Gornji Vakuf, obviously the situation would have changed drastically from this initial briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You can remove this document. And can I have document P 09603 in e-court. Colonel, this was made by your colleague, Christopher Beese, this schematic. It indicates your groups, coordination centres and regional centres and the axes along which you moved. Is this schematic consistent with your perception of the events?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where is the discrepancy, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's where you have Victor 2 and Mike 3 actually represented. Mike 3 was not responsible for the Gornji Vakuf area. Once again, I'm not sure at what point in time this was -- this map represents. Once again, times changed and incidents changed and borders may have in fact changed. Realising that CC Travnik was in Travnik and my area of responsibility during the time I was there was the Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and the Prozor area. Excuse me. And so therefore obviously Mike 3 was not in that location as indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's possible that the organisation changed in the meantime, but Mr. Beese had arrived there slightly earlier than you and was there most of the time that you were there. Anyway, it gives us an overview of the area. Let me ask you two more things. You told us yesterday something about the organisation of your work, communications. I believe that part is clear. But, Colonel, you personally and your colleagues moved as a rule only along major roads, and the only exceptions was when you were escorted by one of the factions. On those occasions you could go to use byroads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct based on the type of vehicle that we were initially issued with and that we were one team. We were also escorted by -- by UNPROFOR in a lot of these cases, and in some case we took a risk --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry to interrupt. I really don't have time for that. You have just -- you have already explained that. I'm only interested in one fact, namely, that you moved only along major roads for the most part, and you never moved by night. I believe you said that as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything we did not move at night. We in fact had occasion to move at night. There were escorts but of varying types, and there were times that we did move without an escort or in an area we had not been to previously for other reasons, which if you wish we can explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that for the most part you moved in daytime?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, when we look at this schematic, and if we project it on the geographic map of the area, I will put it to you that simple arithmetics show that you, the monitors, covered more -- less than 1.5 per cent of the territories where you were active, and I mean by that all the three regional centres. So your movement and your direct knowledge were derived from 1 to 1.5 per cent of the territory. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. In your statement, you dealt in greater detail -- I mean, the statement you gave to OTP investigators, if I may remind you. You said that your main task, and you repeated that in your testimony here, was to gather information, to report to ECMM headquarters in Zagreb and, subsequently, the ministers of the EU countries, but you also had other tasks. You played the role of negotiators or mediators in negotiations. You participated in the distribution of humanitarian aid, because whether you liked it or not, you had to get involved in that job, and you had to get involved in some rescue missions. Is it correct that you were engaged in all of these activities to a greater or smaller extent?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show us document P 01221. That's an exhibit we've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While the document is being placed on the screen, it follows from the document that ECMM Regional Centre Split had 17 teams of monitors for the Republic of Croatia, Montenegro, and south-west Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can we please turn to page 2 of the document. Does this figure sound realistic to you? Is that how you remember the situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What specifically do you want me to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The number of teams of monitors. Do you remember that Regional Centre Split had only 17 teams of monitors that operated in Croatia, Montenegro, and south-western Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's on page 3, because the first one is the facsimile. You will see there Regional Centre Split and in brackets there's a description. Somewhere in the middle. The first sub-heading on the page. "17 monitor teams ..." It's dated 19th of January, that's true, but I put it to you that this situation did not change by May when you arrived. Is that correct? You don't remember, you don't know, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I cannot comment based on the fact that only what you displayed here. If that was in an official report, then I would have to say yes, it was there. I was responsible and in one location. I was not responsible or had the -- the purview of those around me other than those immediately to my left and right flank and my higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question. The Defence is showing you a document dating back to the month of January. You arrived on the 29th of May. That is several months later. So the Judges would like to know if the situation that you found when you arrived was the same as in the month of January, because in this description of the month of January, it -- in the description it says: Because of artillery fire, whether from the Croat side or the Muslim side, the movements around Prozor were limited. When you arrived because I looked at the map between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor there are 12 to 15 kilometres. They are connected by a road with this checkpoint at Makljen. But when you circulated between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor in the period you spent there, was there artillery fire that prevented your movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on my arrival. The situation in Gornji Vakuf was -- had relatively stabilised itself to allow us to move in, remembering the main road in was through Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and then over to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to return to an answer you have given before or agreed to before, namely that you covered roughly or at best 1.5 per cent of the territory. I am not quite sure what this is supposed to signify. Does it mean that you actually -- you set foot or wheel on that part of the territory or that your information was limited to that? Because I can imagine that first when driving you saw large area, so that must have been a relatively considerable part of the territory, and you must have talked to people and the talk was perhaps, it's for you to tell me, not limited to the locality where you were so that maybe one could say intellectually you covered more than 1.5 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- my immediate response is -- was given in trying to understand what the question was. The unfortunate thing, I think this is a question of how long is a piece of string. I'm not sure how much territory I was supposed to cover based on the overall 100 per cent. I know that my area of responsibility during that time frame consisted of the Prozor area, Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno. I did travel between Split and Prozor and of course Gornji Vakuf up to Zenica on occasion and observed other areas or other territories, but once again, in the three months that I was in that particular region my responsibility was those three communities. Is that 1.5 per cent of the overall? I can't answer you, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I -- I don't know whether that was really what -- what counsel meant with this question. I -- I understood counsel as implying that in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Bugojno, which was your area, you only covered 1.5 per cent of that, but maybe that I misunderstood, and then I'm sure Mr. Kovacic will kindly set me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this example that I put to the witness and that was accepted by the witness is based solely on the description of roads along which ECMM monitors moved. We have enough evidence about that from earlier testimony and from Colonel's testimony. So it is pure arithmetics. If we project these roads on which they moved on the geographic map in the around Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor or on the entire map of Bosnia, it doesn't matter, we get the figure of 1 to 1.5 per cent. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this. How do you come up with this figure? Do you make a string of all the roads that are manageable and then you take the portion on which the witness has travelled or -- it's not clear to me as a concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took statistical data about the territory, the area of those municipalities, and I calculated the portion of these municipalities covered by main roads because the witness testified that they only used main roads and, very exceptionally, along byroads. And the witness confirmed it. In fact he said he never used byroads. So it is my assertion, and we can check this with experts, that is the case. This map was prepared by ECMM and it has not been contested. Now, would I like to ask the witness another follow-up question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us yesterday that you were the eyes and ears as far as these events were concerned, but let me remind you that in another case in which you testified as well, Prosecution versus Hadzihasanovic, on page 7594, and I will quote you, you put it in stronger terms, in greater detail: "[In English] We could not be the eyes and the ears everywhere." I emphasise this "everywhere." "But we, and we were only one team in that location, and that responsibility of those three communities." [Interpretation] So in the context of the questions I put to you before, and you said something similar at the beginning of yesterday's testimony, I will ask you the following: Do you agree that your objective possibilities of observation were not good, bearing in mind the territory or the limitations you mentioned, all the jobs you had to do, the number of teams and so on and so forth. Would you agree that objectively you were unable to carry out a thorough monitoring?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this in another one, Colonel. You're a professional soldier. Had you been in a military operation in Bosnia-Herzegovina with your troops, would you have agreed to draw up military plans based on the type of information you had as an ECMM monitor, superficial and unverified information? Would you have embarked on any serious kind of activity?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would make the statement that I would use the resources and the sensors that I had at my disposal as a commander. And even though as a commander I don't see the whole battlefield, I have to use those resources and make my best judgement based on the information I do receive. Where I'm trying to -- to lead you here is the fact that I was, yes, one team, but available to me were many different organisations that gave me that capability to then digest information and then distribute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question of the Defence is very subtle, and you are not exactly answering the point. Counsel is asking you in view of the information at your disposal as a representative of the ECMM, in a military situation, would you have used as a basis the same information you had for a military mission? That is the question. All this is in order to test the reliability of your information. So as a military operative, would you have embarked on a military mission with the information that you had at the time, rather than a civic or civil mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to avoid answering specifically the question, but once again I draw your attention to the real reason I was there. I was not there in a military capacity of trying to do military operations. I would probably approach it in a much different manner. The point being is that information was gathered from a variety of places. I was one monitor. I had UNPROFOR nearby. I had NGO. I had other humanitarian organisations. I had each of the sides. I worked with the politicians. I worked with the civil authorities. I worked with the military. And that whole picture enabled me to make appropriate judgements. If you ask that if I was to do a military operation in that particular area with those resources, I would say, no, for obvious reasons. I would have my own sensors out there to gather that information. Once again, it's what I was there to do and what I was there to -- what information I was required to take up. This -- this statement that I only travelled the main roads I would disagree with. I did not just travel main roads. I travelled many roads in that location, and I saw many people. So it was an overall assessment. Now, it has got to be obvious that one team in that area would have been insufficient in any operation, but I mean we did the best we could with the resources that we had, and more is always better even in military context.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question on this topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, I understand your standpoint, and in any case, I'm not saying that you, meaning all the ECMM monitors, not you personally, I'm not saying that you did not carry out your role there to the best of your ability and in the best way that you could. There is no doubt about that. We can see what efforts you invested, and we can see what the results are. What I am putting to you is that objectively, and I won't list all the reasons, but objectively, you simply did not have the room to verify each and every piece of information, to check it out, to accept the first piece of information as initial information and then to proceed further. You did try to verify some information, but evidently you were unable to check things to the extent that you would have wished for objective reasons. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Your Honour, I would give over to my client, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. My name is Slobodan Praljak. We have already met, or at least I remember your face very well. I don't know whether you've forgotten mine. Would the usher please put on the ELMO this document. Would you put these and give the witness these markers. Colonel, there's just one thing I would like to ask you. My questions will be very brief, and in order to save time, as we are always short of time, in order to receive as many responses from you as possible, please be brief as you would in a military context. Now, you see this aerial photograph here. You can see Bugojno there. That's Bugojno, yes. Sir, would you please take a marker and indicate if you know where the 15.000 refugees you mentioned moved after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in an offensive operation captured Bugojno in a traditional-type war between two armies. Would you take a red felt tipped pen and mark the route taken by the 15.000 refugees and say how many soldiers there were among them. Would you indicate where the Serb forces were, where the BH army forces were, and where the HVO forces were, and to assist, the south is down from Bugojno. You can see on the left-hand side north, south, east, west and Gornji Vakuf is where the clouds are. And if you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you know, as Mr. Praljak has asked you to do, could you give us the locations where the Serbs were positioned, the ABiH was positioned and the Croats were positioned on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately the map that has been presented to me doesn't represent the whole area. To the north, in fact, were the Serb locations of Bugojno which is not indicated on this map. And the area of Gornji Vakuf is clouded. I can't tell you specifically, you know, where they were situated. And I would obviously need a much larger map in my opinion in order to try to draw out something. Once again, I was not in the intelligence-gathering mode. I could not tell you specifically as per the land exactly where boundaries between brigades and front lines, et cetera. I can give you general impression where I saw on -- what I saw on the ground. I at no time ever marked a map or even had any intention to mark a map because that was not within our responsibility. The -- I can only indicate general arrows of where we believe --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- and the exact route of -- of the Croat forces that left between the area of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, all I can comment on is that it was hearsay that they went east, and I was told -- sorry, correction. They went west into Serb-controlled territory, and they eventually were met up down below. There were -- I was at the location between Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf in which they had come together, and it was a mixture of civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, sir. We heard that yesterday. Colonel, please, Their Honours have to reach a decision as to the guilt or innocence of these men. That is why I only wish to discuss the extent to which your information is precise and exact. If you do not know where the Serb positions were on this map, that is sufficient for my purposes. So please tell me, do you know what the route taken by the refugees was and where the Serb positions were? If you need to use the large map, you have a large map next to you and you may use that. I would like you to understand that my time is very limited, and therefore I have to put precise questions and get precise answers from you to find out what precisely you know. I don't need explanations of why you don't know something. So can you indicate this either on the little map or on the big map next to you, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't indicate the exact route. All I can indicate to you is the direction that they went, which was to the west and then to the south to the Prozor area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Google map. Can't you with a pencil just show us approximately? We have Bugojno here. Gornji Vakuf is in the clouds. Can't you approximately indicate the route they took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a small community between the area of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf which I say I can't tell you because I haven't seen the scale on this map and the exact distances. As I remember correctly, the area between Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf is about 35 kilometres and if we take somewhere halfway in between there -- they were located initially -- and what I'm referring to is the Croats. And then from that location I would suggest the Serbs were up north here around Bugojno and kind of come down like this. Once again, I'm not familiar with the scale. I can't tell you the exact locations and would suggest that they went in this direction here and then south down into Bugojno. A different coloured map here. This direction and then south. Once again, I cannot verify this line here being the exact line other than trying to visualise or see it on -- on a scaled map. And as I -- and from down here, obviously down south here was -- in those days, this was Muslim controlled and this is what I referred to yesterday that was also Croat controlled. Is that what you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness just please mark these lines with S for the Serb line and R for the route taken by the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this diagram does not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, red or black is more easily visible. Thank you. Colonel, thank you very much. This is more or less the exact route taken by the refugees, and this is the cooperation mentioned by the Prosecutor between the Croats and the Serbs. After losing a town and after there being 15.000 refugees, the only way they could find to move along was through Serb territories while all the convoys were moving towards the very army that was causing all this. And you will please look at the next map. It's also a Google map and it shows Gornji Vakuf and Prozor. And while this map is being placed on the ELMO, I wish to ask you the following: Yesterday, you said, and we need not repeat it today, that at that time, which was late July, 1993, 15.000 people arrived in Prozor where at that time there were about 1.900 or one and a half thousand inhabitants. Would that be 10 times more refugees, women, children, men, elderly, than that place had inhabitants? Is the number of people who arrived 10 times larger than the number of people actually living in that place?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the infrastructure or population base was prior to the war, in fact, how many total people were living there. But at the time there was only, as you stated, about 1.500 people who lived there when I was there and with the additional 15.000 that did arrive. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we have the census from 1981, and this did not change a lot. This is from 1981. In the town there were 610 Croats and 1.448 Muslims. So about 2.000 people in total. In view of the war and some people moving out or fleeing, I stand by my question as to whether this was 1.500 people, whereas the number of people who arrived were 15.000. In Paris with the surrounding areas there are 10 million inhabitants, so what would the job of a commander look like? And I was then a commander. If 100 million people were to arrive in Paris, who had been expelled from their homes, who were there with everything with their wives and children, as a soldier can you even imagine such a situation, and then I will move on. Just tell me, can you imagine it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. It's a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll agree. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me whether in the areas where you were moving you ever saw five buses in a single place, five buses of Croatian army or whatever parked on the road? Or five trucks in one place?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had. You must -- I would ask you to give me a time and place as to where I saw those five buses. I saw many buses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: If you can fit 60 people into a bus, how many buses would there have to be to move 15.000 people from that area across Mount Vran, taking the Diamond road as you call it. We called it the "Road of salvation." Would you need 300 buses to move these people out? It's easy to calculate mathematically.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the amount of buses that would be required to move individuals from the area between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor out or from Prozor somewhere else? I'm sorry, I'm not getting what -- what calculation you want me to make and for what reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, you side quite clearly that these people arrived in Prozor, and you indicated on the map what route they took, and you said there were 15.000 of them. We also said there were 1.500 people in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Praljak. The Bench has a problem. We don't quite understand what you are getting at. We know that there were 15.000 refugees that arrived in Prozor. What are you trying to establish, that these 15.000 refugees were transported on 300 buses or trucks, and you want the witness to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said here and the reports show that in late July Bugojno fell in the offensive. We saw what the consequences were. The witness said that the offensive of the BH army continued. We know that 15.000 people arrived in a place where there were 1.500 people. The question that arises is: What is the military commander doing? What are the civilian authorities doing? And this witness, who was monitoring and collecting intelligence, did he ever see in one spot five buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if 300 buses had to be found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. He hasn't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The witness was not collecting intelligence. Mr. Praljak is misleading the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Moreover, Mr. Praljak, we have before us not an expert, but a witness. An expert might be able to say what the commander should do or should not do. The witness can only say what he has seen, heard, smelled, and so forth. So I think your question is not a proper question for a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to put the question in the correct way. If the witness says in his reports how many tanks he saw, if he asks what my military speciality is and so on, and it is not his mandate to ask me that, if he establishes there are offensives and so on, then the witness is talking about facts and gathering information. Secondly, I asked the witness clearly whether he ever saw five buses in a single spot, and the answer can be yes, no, or I don't remember. Five empty buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you seen buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question was not whether you saw them - please assist me - but whether you saw five empty buses parked together in a single place and, if so, where and when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also -- I mean, there is a specific time that I can refer to in which it was evacuation of the area of Rat, which was down the "road to salvation" between Gornji Vakuf and Zenica in which I know that the Croats were evacuating. We in fact escorted those full, initially empty buses, and then full buses of people from that area to an area to the east -- sorry, correction, to the west of -- the direction we went was to the west back to Gornji Vakuf, south from Gornji Vakuf and then between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor we went south or west again to another small town up in the hills at which pointed in time -- Podgradje is in that area or just south of that -- of which we then let the convoy released -- released them into Croat territory. And, yes, definitely more than five buses, and they were loaded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, I simply think we went left, right. There was a village there. That this does not contribute to Their Honours' understanding. But anyway, please look at this map of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor. Yesterday, you said on two occasions, I don't have time to put documents to you now, but you said that on that route you saw HVO soldiers with rifles in their hands overseeing the digging of trenches and that it was Muslims who were digging the trenches to the right and left of the road. I will show you a military map of that area, and please tell me where is that field to the left and right of the road that you were talking about. And I will tell you that Their Honours have also travelled along that road, and both you and I have travelled along it dozens of times. So I will help you see both on this map and a more detailed one that there is not so much as a square metre of field on either side, that this road runs through a valley and that there is a forest on both sides of the road. So please look at the military map, the smaller one. Not this one, the smaller one. Leave the previous map, please. Leave the previous Google map. So the witness can say where going from Gornji Vakuf toward Makljen -- well, first of all, can you tell me where the HVO positions were and where the army of BH positions were so that we know where trenches would have to be dug. Show the witness the military map. Could you put the part between Gornji Vakuf and Makljen on the ELMO so that Their Honours can see too. Please explain to the Judges where the field is, and look at the contour lines and show us where the lines between the HVO and the BH army, which was on the offensive as you say, were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have this map in e-court. It might be easier for everyone to follow. It's 3D 00381. It may be easier for the witness, but it will be easier for everybody else if we look at it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf, Rama, please. Could you pull it down a little bit. Raise it, please. Can you see Prozor? It's less visible here. Can you show us, using the marker, where -- where the demarcation lines with the BH army so that trenches could be dug at all, especially since you say you saw it from a road and that it was in a field. Where do you see a square metre of field between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go to the north of Prozor toward Gornji Vakuf, you can move down the map slightly. The other way. Good. You can see that in the low ground there is in fact a creek that runs through that area or a river, a small river. That area was completely surrounded by --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, where to the north? Could you indicate it? You said between Gornji Vakuf and Rama. Just show us where you had seen it. Time, place. So where do you see a field here, and where are the lines? Where was the BH army in Zdrinci, and where was the HVO? Would you draw in the positions?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, and I don't mean to avoid this, I had no direct military knowledge of any of the positions. That was not my responsibility and I was not in a position to gather that information or keep record of where everybody was on the ground. I can give you a general location --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. We have heard that several times already. Thank you. If you can't draw it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have asked the witness to show where in his view the locations of the -- of the two armies were. Now, he just explained that he had no specific knowledge, but he would like to show to you according to his knowledge where those front lines went. So please allow him to do so what you have asked in the first place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I -- if I may, I'm trying to look as well for time and place as to exactly what you want me to draw. The issue at hand obviously is that the lines changed in that three-month period. We initially saw the line north of Gornji Vakuf and eventually it ended up by the time I left to the south of Gornji Vakuf, and -- and in fact, right beside our headquarters, beside our warehouse, which was the UNPROFOR warehouse, was Zrinko's headquarters. So for obvious reasons at a given point in time, there was occupation within Gornji Vakuf, and I want to draw a line something like this up the valley here, which is the valley we looked at and kind of came down like this. I can't comment -- and at a point in time the "road to salvation" which I believe was -- unfortunately the pen is getting away on me here. Is there a way to erase this, erase some of the lines?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you draw, I would like to say this to the Chamber: I'm not rushing the witness for the sake of rushing, but we have heard so much evidence and so many facts, and I have so little time to clarify facts as precisely as necessary for the Trial Chamber to be able to make a valid judgement on this situation at the time when I was there and when the gentleman was there. If we are going to skip over such things and if I am to have 40 minutes to clarify 15 points that have been explicitly made here, then of course I have to resort to attempts to get "I know" or "I don't know" from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was the demarcation line between HVO and the BH army in the end of July, early August, 1993? The demarcation line between HVO and BH army.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you move the map to the north slightly more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you roll -- scroll the map down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the registrar is telling me that if you move the map upwards, you will lose part of the map at the bottom of the map. So this is a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... possible. Since it is clear that the Colonel does not have precise data about lines, then in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What is this, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to do is come to grips with the time frame in which you're talking about. The line to the north of Gornji Vakuf, which extended up - excuse me - the "road to salvation", was in fact -- one side was controlled by Croats in the south, and to the north was -- was the Muslims. At a given point in time, as I understood -- as time progressed, slowly but surely the BiH eventually controlled the whole of Gornji Vakuf and shoved -- and moved the Croats to the south. Just prior to this time actually occurring, the other circle that I put on the map and which I've now hashed is the flat area that I was referring to which is around the creek bed. And if I'm getting this correctly, this is a 1:100000 map. So each grid square here is about 1 kilometer long. You can see very easily that the flat ground does occur in the area as you approach down into Gornji Vakuf. And it was in this area on the left and right around the creek bed that I observed this. And I fully understand and acknowledge what the General is saying from the perspective all the way up through this area it is restrictive and the contour lines are very, very steep. And you're right, it is forested in that area and it would have been difficult to see except for the high features. So it is this ground here as you approached into Gornji Vakuf that it flattened out and allowed you to see at least 300 to 400 metres in both directions along that creek bed that I recall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel. All this -- if I told you that this was under HVO control all the time and has -- had never been lost, that would be a waste of time. We can Google it again and we would find out there was no flat terrain there, but I don't want to spend any more time on that. Could you please pass this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. There's a contradiction here. Mr. Praljak is saying that the area which you have hashed, which is a bed of the river where you saw people digging trenches, Mr. Praljak said that this area was controlled by the HVO, and you're saying that because of the ABiH offensive the area was then controlled by the Muslims, and this is why you have plotted this line underneath. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The line to the south I'm only assuming went that far south realising that Gornji Vakuf in its entirety was taken by the Muslims in that time frame in my opinion. I said I'm only assuming and I cannot absolutely verify that it went that far south. All I do know is that it was pushed from out of Gornji Vakuf and the area to the north-east of Gornji Vakuf, that whole area was -- was eventually taken over by the BiH. And once again, I cannot answer precisely that this -- this line is absolutely accurate all the way through. It may in fact, as the general's already indicated, stayed to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that Gornji Vakuf was taken by the ABiH. In which month was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the month -- I want to say late July, early August and later on in August. And the reason I know this is because they attacked around us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I had understood that the V2 office was based in Gornji Vakuf. When the ABiH attacked, did you leave your office or did you stay in that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in location and actually witnessed the battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you saw the battle unfold. When a warring party occupies the territory, do they mark the territory? I assume that the ABiH was controlling the road. Did you ever see any ABiH checkpoints and, if so, could you indicate which ones these are on the map, because when you take up a position, you control that position and you control the roads. Did the ABiH establish any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were check points. Initially there were checkpoints between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor, which -- which moved literally day by day, and you could literally see wherever the new checkpoint was, then it would move further south and further south, and eventually it was absorbed into the Gornji Vakuf area and therefore from the August time frame there was no checkpoints between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor proper. The checkpoints started to appear on the south side of Gornji Vakuf and the road over to Zenica. Once again, I have to see the whole map here to get whatever that road was over to the eastern side to get an understanding that in fact the feature that I may -- I mean, this road up here to the north may be the wrong road and may in fact be this it one here that's the one to Zenica. I'm not sure. But on this side, all up here, I got the appearance it was controlled, and all the way up the valley here. And this was the valley we knew stuff was happening, and the Croats were up in this area. If that clarifies the situation. The road -- the road definitely over to Zenica had -- had eventually BiH checkpoints, but -- and just to put it in perspective, the Makljen was always, in my time, controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a quick point, Your Honour, because later on I assume that this is going to be moved into evidence. Perhaps during the break the gentleman could just mark it and then when we go back on record indicate the marks, what all these lines denote, otherwise, months from now we won't be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We shall now have a 20-minute break. Time is up. If you could mark this map during the break this would be useful to all of us. We shall resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please be so kind as to sign this map so that we can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can you mark today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 37, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you now please put on the ELMO the Google map that I have shown before, the Google map of Gornji Vakuf and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now, Colonel, please indicate on that map the exact spot where you saw Muslim prisoners digging trenches under HVO. The Google map, please. We can't see it. On the ELMO, please. Here it is. Just indicate the spot, please, where you saw the incident of trench digging. Put a date and sign it, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am to assume that this is -- what I'm indicating here is the road down to Prozor -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now please sign it and put a date.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 38, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm trying to come to grips with this here. This does not look right. This is the town of Gornji Vakuf where the dot is indicated on Google, and then this is the road down to Prozor? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the road towards Prozor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this location here. So it's outside Prozor to the south along that road on the left and right, and this is that area that is flat and goes up against the ridge-line on the left that I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. The flat area. We can see that, that there is no flat area there, in fact, but we'll deal with it later. Please tell us, you said -- you said at one point that the BH army took over Vakuf. Do you remember on which date, on which day it was? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember the date. And if I can recant on my information I provided that I thought that Gornji Vakuf fell. It was probably incorrect. In reflection, all I can remember is that Gornji Vakuf was divided, and it was right down the centre of the town of which, if you look to the south-west area which was controlled by the -- by -- in my opinion the HVO, and of course the north-east and down to the road in the north, and I'm referring to, if I may again, this area down in here. If anybody can see that. Sorry, I've got the wrong finger going here. Thank you. So what I'm referring to is -- is a line something like that, and then eventually it came on and dropped down like this. The -- if the road -- if there is a road over this way towards Zenica, and I think this may have been it over here, and I'll just mark the road like that, if I remember correctly, and this -- this kind of line that got -- and this kind of moved in that direction, if I'm not mistaken. But there is major activity all up there if that's what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, there is no road to Zenica there at all. It's a non-existent track, in fact, towards Pojnica [phoen]. The road to Zenica is in fact straight to the top towards Bugojno, but we don't have time for that now. I have to note simply that you are not aware of the military situation except in very general terms, and you wrote in your statement that the BH army attacked Vakuf in that offensive. And will you please look at that map indicating Neretva 93 that began at your -- in your time, and tell us when you look at that map, do you know anything about that open war between Croats and Muslims, about the activities? Behind you is the map. On that board behind you is the map.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what do you want me to indicate on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware, are you familiar with the overall activities, the military activities of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the HVO while you were performing your honourable duties there? Just look at the map and tell me if you know anything about it, what you know? And if you don't know anything, you can just tell me, "I don't know," and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've ever seen this map in this amount of detail. I had a map that indicated front lines on the day from 1993, but that was the extent of it. I'd have to take a very close detail. I understand map symbols and I understand what is being portrayed there but I'd have to take a look at everything to see what you're trying to portray here. Once again, to ask me whether I knew the detail and specifically where every location is, I have to answer no, I did not. Once again, we were not in that business.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir -- Colonel, would you please be so kind as to assist me. My question is a very precise, a military question, and you are a colonel of the Canadian army. According to this map, were you familiar with the overall conflict, the open war between two armies in end July, in August, and in September when you were there? Do you know about that? And if you don't know anything about it, you can tell me so. Look at the map and tell me in military terms what you knew, how much you knew. If you were not aware of it, just tell me so and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when I left the area to return home on leave that the situation was relatively stable. When I returned some two weeks later the situation had completely changed, and I knew there was an offensive happening from the ABiH moving south from the north and that it eventually ended up with two opposing sides going at each other, for lack of a better term right now, to -- on the battlefield. One in the south, HVO, and the north being BiH. That I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Could you please indicate on that map you marked the road towards Zenica, put a date and your signature on the map that we see on the ELMO. Just indicate the direction towards Zenica. You drew in the road.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Once again, I need to see the complete map here. If I had the indication then I can draw where Zenica is and I can draw you that road back. I need the map to the north of this in order to indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you cannot testify that what you drew in here is actually the road to Zenica. This has nothing to do with the road to Zenica, or does it, what you just drew on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest if I may draw this back -- if I were to look at the map and if I remember the map of the day there was in fact another map sheet to the north which we used. And as he indicated on this map here there is Novi Travnik, 25 kilometres. So if we take that, and I'll refer to this -- this road here as that road that made lead up to Zenica and not in fact this one down to the south. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Cross out this lower one, draw the one up north towards Zenica, and write Z for Zenica, and erase that.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Is there anything else you wanted added?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, nothing. Thank you. Just put your date and the signature. What is this thing to the right that you just drew? Would you explain?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. You drew something to the right in the red marker. What is it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this -- this may have ended up, and I'm just -- sorry. I'll get the eraser going here again. Once again, I'm trying to come to grips with the actual lines at the time that I was now leaving the mission area, and I do believe that once again Gornji Vakuf was still divided, and HVO controlled this area which I'm indicating down to the south. And obviously ABiH was in the north. So that, I believe, may have been the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the area covered by BH army in green.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that in blue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Blue is fine.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please write "ABH" and "HVO" below that.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's fine thank you. "ABH".

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And "HVO" in red, and put a date and signature, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit IC 39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: A short question. Do you know how large were the contact lines on the front line between ABiH and HVO? What was the length of the contact lines? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another question that will be a complex one. You told me you don't know the exact date when Vakuf fell. It is true that HVO lost all lines on one day. We'll establish later which day. Were those lines lost for -- in one day? How many people fled from the area of Vakuf on that day, 5.000 or 6.000? Did HVO forces blow-up warehouses with food and weapons? Was livestock killed by HVO forces, and did people torch 25 of their own homes when they were fleeing? And is it the case that all those lines were recovered by the evening of the same day, and is it true that I recovered those lines in that famous film with Sylvester Stallone? Have you heard anything about that incident at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific date that I believe you're referring to, the loss of Gornji Vakuf, was the date where in fact the ABiH attacked around our warehouse, and that evening I can remember prior to the fall of that particular headquarters in which Zrinko was located, I remember showing up with -- I refer to one of your battle buses which had stretchers on board and it was an armoured bus that could take up to 30 people if I remember correctly. And we got the phone call that something was up, and at that point in time we moved the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, please. Those are details, and please don't take exception, but those are the details that I'm not interested in right now. The things that I have put to you, are they accurate to the best of your recollection? Do you know or don't you know? Just tell me. Just tell me. Are you aware of whether those things I put to you are true? Do you know about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I put a very proper question. Mr. Prosecutor, my question was very proper. Is this gentleman aware of those facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Praljak put a number of questions to the witness, and he requests one response, yes or not. Maybe yes, maybe not. It's unfair to the witness to conduct in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, ask one question after another, step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you don't know how long the lines were. Do you know that in one day, in the morning, all lines of the HVO fell and were abandoned? Do you know that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the area that I was in that event had happened, because the next morning the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Colonel. Do you know how many people fled together with the army towards Prozor on that day? Do you know how many people fled together with the army on that day towards Prozor? Step-by-step. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only comment on the area which I was in, which was Gornji Vakuf. Yes, I did know that there was a number of people that did move from the Prozor down to do -- or sorry, from Gornji Vakuf down to Prozor, because they were not there the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that I, climbing on top of a tank, lead the army back, and that same evening I had recovered all HVO positions and had them under my control? So they were back in that position again the next day. Just give me a yes or no, Colonel. Don't beat about the bush.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You made me aware of that 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to dwell any more on Vakuf. Could you please put this paper with that large Tuzla convoy on the ELMO. The paper that I drew about the convoy. I just have a couple of questions concerning the convoy. As for this map that the gentleman did not recognise, the big one on the panel behind, could it be exhibited, please? Yesterday, Colonel, you told us about the length of the Tuzla convoy. This one. Yes. Right. Just can we see it all, in its entirety. Thank you. You stated yesterday that 500 trucks set out from Split and that on the move they were 200 metres from each each other and that the whole length was 14 kilometres and something. So according to my calculations, if the distance between trucks is 200 metres, then the whole convoy is 100 kilometres. If the -- if the distance between them is 100 metres, then length is 50 kilometres. And if the distance is only 30 metres, then the whole convoy is 15 kilometres long. Can you confirm that? You said yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Understood. Now, with the understanding that I gave you an average of 200 metres. If there was 200 metres. Sometimes there may have been 10 or 15 metres. These are not disciplined military drivers that would keep that standard 200 metres between each vehicle for security reasons. I mean, this was a large convoy that moved en masse from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we know that the convoy moves from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I think there is an error in B. It should be 100, not 200.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that corrected, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber misses nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So, Colonel, convoys move from one place to another. I can also ask a question, what if the stars rise and then set. Hamlet gives speeches and then blah, blah. We are now dealing with exact data. The convoy set out from Split, 500 trucks, with three escorting vehicles. Where is the army on earth that would allow one convoy to set out at the moment when the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina took over Travnik and when that number of refugees was moving away from Travnik? How many refugees were moving from Travnik southwards, and why were there only three UNPROFOR escorting vehicles with the convoy consisting of 500 trucks.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, there are specific instructions from our higher headquarters, and I'm referring to UNPROFOR as well as our own, that this convoy was made up of locals of Tuzla from all sides and we were not to become involved. Once again, it was a situation where we inherited this large number of vehicles coming into our area. We -- we were, in fact, the ones that stopped -- may I continue or -- or is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We've heard all that yesterday. There's no need. I would allow you, but there's no need. Do you know that Travnik fell at that moment, looking from the Croatian side? Did you know that at that precise moment the HVO lost Travnik and do you know how many refugees and troops were moving from -- fleeing from Travnik south?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of that because we had been informed that things had gone -- there was now a battle between us and where they needed to get to, and that is one reason we stopped the convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please be so kind as to correct the number 2 into a number 1 under B, please. Thank you very much. Thank you. You worked with UNPROFOR. Would you tell us whether UNPROFOR had a mandate, 500 metres to the left of the road and 500 metres to the right of the road prescribed for the passage of a convoy, and I will put it on the ELMO. They had the right to use weapons to defend the convoy. Was this defined in the UNPROFOR mandate, that it had the right to use firearms to protect the convoy moving along that road?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically the mandate of UNPROFOR in those days. I know, however, that convoys were being directly threatened coming up that road and eventually it came to the point in time where return fire could be used if convoys, and I'm referring to UNHCR convoys, were threatened.
