And their responsibility were UNHCR, not other humanitarian organisations. And they eventually ended up taking on responsibility for the escort of those UNHCR once there entered our region, and hence that's why many of the resources of Graham Binns's company were spread thin throughout that area and during that time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now move on to talk about the Croatian army and some other matters you raised here. So could we please have 3D 0047. That's a CD. And could you show those two documents to the gentleman. Could you please put those two documents, the "Road to salvation did --" no. We'll do it after the CD. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see me in Capljina. Stop here, please. And you will see that I have a German flag on my pullover. Stop. You see? It's the German flag. And -- well, it can easily be seen. From the fact that you saw a German flag on my pull over, would you conclude that I was a German soldier in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had not met you before, ever, once again, I would not consider you a German because I have not seen your full uniform or I had not spoken to you. I mean, just by having a German pullover with a flag I could not assume you were a German. I would have to see the pants you were wearing or if you had any beret or headdress. But I cannot jump to the conclusion that you're a German.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct. So the fact that whether an army is present on a certain territory or not can be ascertained in principle by the mission of that army, its task, its orders, the route it is to take, the tasks it is to perform. So would you then agree with me that when you come across a soldier in Gornji Vakuf and you see an HV insignia on him, it does not necessarily mean he is a Croatian soldier from Croatia. What it means is purely that he's wearing a jacket with HV on it. Would you agree with me that one would need more information than that to ascertain that the Croatian army was present on a certain territory?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with your statement, but realising once again you'd have to look at in its entirety. If you take an isolated patch and say he is a Croat soldier or he's a German soldier, I would probably say that would be impossible without seeing the first picture. It is my opinion that I saw many soldiers with HV. They showed up at a time and place where you would probably expect them because of the offence that -- the offensive that was taking place at that particular time on the ground, and uniforms were relatively new and they were relatively in a lot better shape than the HV uniforms I had traditionally seen on the ground during that time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you say that when you see a new uniform the soldier is a Croatian soldier, and when you see someone in an old shabby uniform he's an HVO soldier. I won't go into this any further. On page 9 of your report, I'll read out what you say. It's page 9. Of your statement, sorry. The statement you made, in the middle and I'm quoting: "On that day in Prozor, I saw one soldier with a HOS patch on his soldier, two soldiers with HVO patches on their shoulders, and four soldiers with an HZ on a red and white chequerboard on their shoulder. In my belief, these soldiers were part of the Croatian army which was incorporated into the HVO forces." Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have the exact wording.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: One HOS soldier, two soldiers with HV patches, and four soldiers with an HZ patch, which I'm not familiar with, are sufficient for you to conclude and sign this piece of information that you believe that the Croatian army had been incorporated into the HVO forces. Would you just say whether this is the statement you made? Is what I have read out correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can give me a time and date as to that statement. I also do not have it here in front of me. I cannot verify whether I made it or did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 17th of June, I don't know when you gave the statement -- oh, yes. Here it is. The 9th and 10th of October, 2001. And the day when you saw this was on the 17th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once between, that would be directly related to a piece -- or a documentation I would have written or made reference to. If this is a statement that you have that I made and it is in fact confirmed I made that statement, then I cannot deny and say, yes, that is correct. May I also make the observation that military officers in wrong uniforms are in violation, I believe, of a convention. I'm not sure, and I would have to go and -- I would have to ask that. This is why militaries tend to wear their own uniform and their own patches because they are identifiable from that perspective, and you can assume that that is in effect worldwide. I made that comment. I would not be wearing --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: General Praljak, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I am a bit worried about the time frame of our hearings this morning. Let me remind you that the Defence was given altogether three and a half hours for -- for doing its job. Now I recall that you, General Praljak, you had taken one hour this morning, and -- and I also would like to refer to the fact that Mr. Poryvaev has finished his examination-in-chief in 20 minutes this morning, which all in all would give to the Defence around four or a bit more than four hours for doing the cross-examination. And of course it would be only in a way welcome if we could finish the -- listening to this witness -- Colonel -- witness here today because we are having other witnesses scheduled for tomorrow and for Thursday. So therefore I would like to ask the Defence really to see to it that the time remaining would be -- would be in a way usefully used, and since also we heard this morning that actually Mr. Coric would like to have more time than originally envisaged. So I would really ask all of you to take care of this -- to take care of those remaining hours and to divide among yourselves as discussed and as agreed upon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In addition, you used one hour, 32 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have been given time by the other gentlemen, and I'm adhering to the amount of time I have been given. However, I stand by my opinion that what matters is not that we hear 500 witnesses but that we learn the truth, and the conclusions -- examine the conclusions of the witnesses on which my fate depends. I repeat that I wish to know what I have been found guilty of in the end. And when a Colonel of the Canadian army comes here, who is an expert and who has put forth an incredible number of facts in the documents he has presented, I need to check this. If he has seen a total of four soldiers, one many whom was a HOS soldier who was under the command of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time and he concludes on this basis that the Croatian army was there, we are on very slippery ground. That is why I wish to check the standpoints and conclusions presented. I will go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 13 of the same statement, on I quote, you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour. Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Chamber has given you one hour. You have already had 1 hour, 32. We understand very well what you're saying. The issue of HV, since the witness has explained that according to him there was an HV presence there, you are certainly not going to change his mind, or maybe you are, but try to ask him synthesised questions, and please indicate how much more time you need, because we have another Defence team to intervene on the very important question of the military police, and there are other Defence teams as well, and we have 3 hours 45 in total.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll conclude very quickly. I cannot change the Colonel's opinion, nor is that my intention. I just want to point out on the basis of what information he arrived at what piece of information. He says "after our return we saw HV soldiers in Gornji Vakuf where we had never seen them before. I don't know how many of them there were, but they were wearing HV uniforms."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, is it possible for a colonel in a professional army not to note down the basic information of how many there were? So how is it you don't know how many soldiers of the Croatian army, as you say you saw? Please be brief so we can conclude this quickly.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I would suggest that it was my -- my limited and restricted movement within that area that did not allow me to count every trench with every soldier with every officer to add up to companies, battalions, et cetera. I observed soldiers with certain patches. Those numbers I'm -- on that day I have no understanding as to why I did not indicate the numbers. I would normally indicate those numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on. Thank you. Thank you very much. It's not that I don't think you wish to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Praljak, the Chamber is minded to stop you now because you have already exceeded your time. What is the last useful question for your case, if you have one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honours, the Defence of General Petkovic will give most of its time to General Praljak, so that General Praljak can use 20 minutes of our time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need so much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you the following: Document P 09658 and P 09665, the first is of the 23rd of August, 1993, and the next one is of the 6th of August, 1993. And P 09620 of the 30th of August, 1993. At the time of the fiercest attacks by the BH army on Vakuf, in all three documents you include the following sentence: "UNPROFOR convoys are passing through Gornji Vakuf." And in the second document of the 6th of August you say the convoys are passing through Gornji Vakuf and on -- in the third document, the 30th of August, 1993, the convoys are passing through Gornji Vakuf and in another document you say it was between 50 and 100 trucks per day. I won't waste time showing you all those documents but it's in there very clearly in all three documents so we'll only be wasting time. So who do you think under such circumstances made it possible for the convoys to pass through, and what was the role of Slobodan Praljak, HVO commander, in all that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Colonel. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I think the witness should be shown at least a single document Mr. Praljak means now to contest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Document P 09658, please. The first paragraph, "General situation," line 3: "UNPROFOR convoys passed through Gornji Vakuf without any problems."

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me who insured their security, General?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it's usual in such a military conflict for convoys to be passing through the place where the conflict is taking place, and they are taking everything that is needed by the army, which is carrying out an aggression against me. So what kind of strength do you need to let such convoys pass through in such a situation. And can you give me an example of any war, between France and Germany, between Germany and England, the war in the Baltic, along the Pacific, where such things happened? The next document is P 079665. Can it be put on the ELMO while we are hearing the witness's reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The document which you've just used, the other documents show the same thing. You've heard the question. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all say the same, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially I would like to make a statement based on my -- on your last comment on history. I'm sure there are many examples in many wars where humanitarian aid was moved back and forth between the front lines uninterupted but negotiated. The thing I would like to indicate at that time is that by that time all convoys that were coming up from Split were in fact under the escort of -- of Graham Binns's company which he had to dedicate resources to. In fact, from the point in time that they entered our area, platoons would be assigned to them to run them through our area and then take them on to -- and pass them off further north. The indication was is that prior to that happening, convoys were threatened daily. So with the presence of UNPROFOR with armoured vehicles that would return fire against anybody that actually fired on the convoys, I think that was incentive enough why convoys were left alone as they passed through, realising and understanding that the battle of the day was not conducted on that route.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, I only wish to say that I arrived there on the 26th, and for the most part after that there were no problems with the passage of convoys as you testified to in all your reports. These convoys, let it be said, could have been stopped when entering Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the territory up to Gornji Vakuf was controlled by the HVO all the way from the border. So they demonstrate the attitude of the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, here is a statement by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My last question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Praljak has concluded. Do you agree with what he said or not? He said that when he arrived on that location there was no problem with the passing through of convoys. Do you agree with this or not, or do you have a different view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm starting to recollect that in fact I may even have talked to the general about this on -- on a meeting that we may have had about, you know, unrestricting the convoys, allowing them through. I may have. It's starting to come back to me based on what he is saying. And I would suggest that that may be one of the reasons the convoys were allowed to get through. But I must re-emphasise they were under the escort of UNPROFOR, and I would suggest that that also ensured -- UNPROFOR did not make a habit of running checkpoints. If they had been stopped, they would stop and wait until it was negotiated. And by that time, by indication on my reports, we were moving convoys through unobstructed but they were still being escorted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Their Honours know about the order of the 31st of July. Of course it's easy to write an order. It has to be carried out, but we'll deal with that in a different way. Colonel, I wish to thank you. I would have more questions about multiple rocket launchers, the tanks you spoke about. You said there were three tanks there. I would like to discuss fuel, because we can agree that tanks can be fuelled where they are. They're not taken 10 or 15 kilometres into the rear to refuel. But, Colonel, we had an excellent cooperation up there. We had very nice meetings where we talked about things that were not purely military, and not for a single moment had I doubted your best intentions. I only wanted to establish here the precision of what you saw and then the precision of what can be concluded from what you saw, so that all of us and primarily Their Honours can arrive at the truth of these events. Thank you very much. And thank you very much, Your Honours. Please accept my apologies and gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good morning. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney-at-law from Zagreb. In these proceedings I appear for the Defence of General Milivoj Petkovic. I have reduced my cross-examination to several topics which I feel are important for a good understanding of the context. I believe that based on the documents shown by the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday, which I will show you again if it should prove necessary, we can clarify some important circumstances. To begin with, could my learned friends give to the witness the set of documents that were shown to the witness yesterday to avoid wasting time. Oh, the witness has them. Thank you very much. First of all, I'm interested in the mood of the Muslim population and individual commanders of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect to the peace processes under way at the time of your mandate in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For this reason, I would ask you to look at P 04440. This is a report, a daily report shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel, you have the floor. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am attorney-at-law from Zagreb, and I appear for Mr. Valentin Coric in these proceedings. Sir, we heard in your testimony yesterday, and I believe you will remember that, that you believe there was a direct military connection between the military police in Prozor and the OZ commander. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the military connection, would that connection be a chain of command like we have military police, the commander of that military police, and after that we have the operative zone and the commander of the operative zone? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was set up in a traditional military structure, the -- and if it was the size of a platoon, which is what I am assume -- assuming, then the structure would naturally lead that the MP police commander would be indirectly responsible directly to the OZ commander being a brigade commander. There maybe several platoons of military police throughout his area, but it would be directly within the chain of command in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have in e-court a Defence exhibit, 5D 00538. There it is. Could you please tell us, sir, we see here in the heading "Operative zone, North-west Herzegovina." Is it from what you know the operation zone where Prozor was?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you tell me that, then that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we move, please, to the last page of the document to see the signature. We see that it is signed "Commander Colonel Zeljko Siljeg."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Would you be so kind to tell us precisely on which page and which paragraph we can find what you are referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing I referred to, "Operation zone," is to be found on the first page, just after the description of the stamp on the left-hand side. And the signature is on the last page, on the right-hand side. Just before the words "To," and the indication of addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you seen the signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that the same gentleman that was referred to already today as the commander of the operation zone? I believe it was in -- in the examination-in-chief that he was mentioned again.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am to assume that. Once again, not seeing his picture or a direct comparison, I only can state what I see in front of me is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we please go back to page 1 again. Both versions, Croat and English. Can we just raise the English version a little to see the second paragraph that begins with the words "The meeting -- the following matters were reviewed at the meeting." And point 1 is "Organisation and tasks of the military police." For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I will just put some points from this document to the witness and ask him a couple of questions. Now, in the English version can we move to -- let me find the page. Page 2, last paragraph. And in the Croatian version it's also page 2, paragraph 1, or point 1. I will start reading. "The operations zone commander presented the main problems regarding the formation, control and command of the Military Police. According to the plan of the OZ S/ZH organisation and establishment structure, the 2nd Military Police Battalion is also under it's command in this operation zone, and supply, formation and training is carried out by the Military Police Administration. In their areas of responsibility, brigades can use military police units that have been formed in their areas of responsibility. Military police platoons in brigades are formed by each brigade that supplies and trains them and according to the chain of control and command they are exclusively within the jurisdiction of the brigades." And just one more bit from the next paragraph on the next page. Somewhere in the middle of that paragraph, line three or four. So paragraph 1 in English, it says: "Military Police Platoon commanders --" it goes like this: "In the implementation of military police tasks, a military police battalion commander is directly subordinate to the operations zone commander, and military police platoons in brigades carry out the orders of the brigade commander within their jurisdiction." I'm through with this document, and I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. This document -- the Defence counsel of the accused has just shown you a document which you did not know anything about. She explained to you that there were the 2nd Battalion of the military police and that each brigade is responsible for its own military police units. Do you agree with which -- with everything that was read out to you by Defence counsel? And then your perception of the situation given the job you had and given the fact that you were there as an observer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is described in this letter is for all intents and purposes what I tried to make an initial stab at, what I thought the organisation of -- any standard military organisation would be. There is a technical chain of command, i.e., the military police talking to one another as well as an operational chain of command, which would allow commanders to command their MP platoons. In this case a brigade had an MP platoon. In other cases it may be as big as a company. And in turn would answer to a higher technical chain being the military police battalion. This is -- I'm very familiar with this sort of a structure, and I would have -- and once again, I would have assumed what I really started to talk about, and this is confirmed by this piece of paper, that I am correct. It was set up in a standard military fashion and the control of military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On page 7 of the document in English, in point 4, we're going to give the floor to all people in charge of the brigades. The commander of the Rama Brigade, there are two of them. We can see there. Marinko Beljo will describe the lines facing the Serbs. I think everything is calm and peaceful. A number of problems have arisen due to the Muslims in some villages. And in one settlement there's -- there are five Croatian families that had to move out. The conclusion of this commander was to say that there are no further problems. This document is a document that's dated in the month of March. You arrived after that, and you could see what was happening in Prozor after that. According to you, the Rama Brigade commander, would he have reached the same conclusion in May, June, and July? Would he have mentioned this to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I've lost your train of thought here. I'm not quite sure what you're trying to ask me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall sum up. The commander of the Rama Brigade intervenes, and he takes stock of the situation, and he says there are no problems. But this meeting is held in March, on the 9th of March. And you arrived after that, a few months later. According to you, if this type of meeting had been held in May, June, or July of 1993, would the person in charge of the military police or the Rama Brigade, would he have said the same thing and said that there were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he would not. He would probably have painted a very different sort of picture in that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. I will repeat because I see there's no interpretation. Let me go back to your testimony of yesterday where you described your contacts with the imam of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony you described one event saying that you tried to visit the imam but you were prevented from doing so by the military police.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session now, because I would like to produce one Prosecution exhibit that was shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat my question? Would you agree with me about the Tuzla convoy, that it was privately arranged? It was not organised by any of the humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Privately arranged from the point of view that, as I understood it, it was made up of -- of those of the population of the Tuzla area, because, and I think I already made this statement yesterday, because they had been running out of supplies. No formal aid agency or organisation was bringing stuff in, so they took it upon themselves to run trucks out to the coast, to the area of Split, and to purchase what supplies they could, which included fuel. And I'll just add that this movement took place over almost a one-month period actually before they got loaded and came back in. There was not a large influx of -- of trucks in our -- in our area on the way down. They either moved down in small packages or acquired additional trucks down in Split, but when they were all filled, there was the mass move of one complete convoy from the -- from the west into the east up toward Tuzla as a complete entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From that one might conclude that it was a spontaneously organised convoy arranged by private persons who needed aid.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to come to an understanding what's private and what's public in reference to aid convoys. It was organised by those of -- of that area to get help, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was not organised by any of the organisations that normally handle the gathering and distribution of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, please: Do you know if this convoy was announced and, if so, to whom and when? Was it notified to any of the authorities on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got word of the convoy via our own means and UNPROFOR means, that they were gathering in Split and heading in our direction, and -- and that's why we almost were in a situation of -- of literally hearing on a daily basis were they coming, were they not coming. Once again, we had not taken on responsibility for the convoy whatsoever, either in the Split region or all the way through. It was through our communications that we kept -- we were kept abreast as this large convoy moved in our direction, because it was my opinion that the convoy was being actually formed once things were ready. And I'll put also on the plate that we had the situation to the north of us that had deteriorated. In fact, a battle was now going on. In the meantime this thing was forming up and starting to move in our direction. If I remember, the group down south to us were actually feeding this other 100 trucks or 200 trucks, now 300, now 400, and it kind of went up in chunks of a hundred to eventually give us that 500 plus number of vehicles moving in our direction. So this thing built over a long period of time. To say that it was ad hoc, well, you know, ad hoc over a long period of time, which was, you know, finally became this very large convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From what you just said, should I conclude that the organiser of the convoy did not notify the number of vehicles, the personnel of the convoy, the contents of the convoy, or the destination to you or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it became known as the Tuzla convoy, so we obviously knew where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm asking you. I'm sorry, that's not what I'm asking. I'm asking whether before it became known that a heap of trucks was headed your way whether anybody, monitors, the authority, UNPROFOR or anybody else notified that you that a huge convoy was coming from Split headed there and there, with so many people, with shipment documents, bills of lading, et cetera. Did you know any of these things in advance, or did you find out when the convoy was already on the way?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not get any shipment documents. We did not have the time nor the wherewithal to worry about shipping documents and lading bills. This was in the middle of the war. That we had heard through our chain that these trucks were moving in our direction. Once again I'm reminded of our situation that the responsibility of UNPROFOR was the security of UNHCR convoys, and after a while we became responsible and UNPROFOR, the company, Graham Binns's company, we became responsible for a portion of the route to salvation to conduct escort. Now, that included anything that was moving on that road, and then that was from NGOs to other humanitarian organisations. Once again, it was an issue of inheriting this very large convoy in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me, please, when you reached that convoy or, rather, it arrived in your zone of responsibility, you are around the convoy, you and UNPROFOR, I'm not going to insist on dates, did you and UNPROFOR check the shipment, what exactly was on the trucks, and which persons were on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll describe that -- or I'll very briefly refer to the very first day that we came upon them, realising that we had been waiting out on the road for them for quite some time, and our first real contact with them was at that Prozor road junction in which vehicles were being hived off, and from that point forward we were with the convoy I think for almost up to a week, of which we began to talk to the drivers and realise what sort of cargo they were carrying. This is one of reasons why we made a direct or one of the reasons why our superiors made the direct observation that we should not get ourselves involved because we could not verify what was the content of every vehicle, especially 500 of them. I have no idea, I cannot categorically state right now what was in every truck. What I can state, it appeared to be all foodstuffs, supplies, fuel, that were moving into that direction. And I will not verify one way or the other whether or not there was in fact ammunition, weapons, or whatever. I personally did not see any driver, any co-driver, any family member of that convoy carry anything. No weapons were on that convoy that were visible, and they were totally unarmed. There was, and I believe it may have been a local official that was the individual that we had direct contact with who also was the kind of guy in charge of the convoy from their perspective. There was no armed guards present on the convoy. They were a bunch of civilians trying to make out in a very unfavourable situation to get home, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have a break now. We shall have a 15-minute break and resume at a quarter to 1.00 and then we will have one hour left. I hope that we will have finished in the remaining hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I think we established before the last break that you did not inspect the convoys but that you learned information about what the convoys contained and what persons were in it from the drivers and other persons in the convoy. Continuing on from this, I will ask you the following: Would I be right in saying that at the time the convoy was passing through the area there was fighting going on around Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and that's why we stopped the convoy in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say that you stopped the convoy, yesterday you said that at Makljen you could not pass through that. Passage was denied to you. So did you stop the convoy at Makljen because of the fighting around Travnik, or was it somebody else who stopped it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a situation that we began to understand what it was up against. I can remember personally talking to the lead vehicle, which I believed contained the leader of the convoy, if you want to call it that. I remember explaining him the situation that unfortunately a battle had broken out between him and Tuzla, and that my recommendation would be, you know, to hold tough until "we could release the convoy," and we would be receiving that information from our higher headquarters through a cease-fire or whatever. We explained the dangers that that may be ahead for this convoy if they were to proceed. So we gave them advice, and from that point actually made the recommendation to them. Once again, it was left up to them to decide whether to proceed or not proceed. All we did was presented what we knew as the fact, which was there was a battle up front. "You're going to run into trouble. Are you sure this is where you want to be or take these people?" And slowly but surely we began to take --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, for interrupting you. We are very short of time. Could we conclude, then, that this convoy was stopped pursuant to an agreement between you and the people in the convoy? I believe the answer to be yes, so could you please just confirm and we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, please tell me, it was from your conversations with these persons that you learned that the cargo was intended for Tuzla and for the civilian population of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that beforehand as this thing started to build out of Split and come in our direction. It was obviously confirmed when we started talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who did you learn it from? Excuse me for interrupting you. Who did you learn that from? Did you see the documents?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from my chain of command. Either -- and what I'm referring to is, you know, through the daily report procedures that this convoy was down there, conversations with the -- likely the team down toward Tomislavgrad, through UNPROFOR. Of course they were getting word of it up their chain that this thing was building, with the realisation that their responsibility in those days was that piece of route was within their sector. So it was from a variety of locations that we did receive this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you do not know for sure from what source, from whom, and when?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we first heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, when you first heard about it, who told you, and whoever told you, did they tell you how they had ascertained that, that is where the convoy was going and for whom it was intended? And if they learned that from the participants in the convoy, was that information checked and verified and in what way?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would suggest that what needed to -- what we need to understand is probably somewhere in one of my daily reports would be an indication of when I first heard about it, realising that we were going to inherit this convoy or was going to come into our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you can't recall right now?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To name a specific time and place, no, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, you're a soldier, so -- and a very well-educated and well-trained soldier. So please tell us, a convoy of 500 vehicles arrived in a war theatre. There was fighting nearby. Had you been the commander of that area - and this is a hypothetical question - would you have wanted to check what was in the convoy, check the contents of those trucks, in view of the fact that the convoy was passing through your area and then would be passing through enemy-held territory, which would mean that there was a possibility it would bring supplies to those enemy forces? Would you wish to see what the convoy contained? Would that be normal for you to check that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be normal, and I -- and I would -- if I may. I would be checking, and I did check. My statement was initially made that I did not check every single vehicle. This convoy was made up of all three ethnic groups, Serb, Muslim, and Croat, that were in this convoy, including children and wives or females of the drivers that was moving in that direction. I -- over a one-week period that this convoy was in my location, I began to understand and to know what this convoy was made up of. I inadvertently would check back the vehicles by -- and I remind you I spent time with them, by sitting in the middle of the convoy on one night as I explained, and during the day I would be sitting with them and I would be talking through my translator and get a feel for the -- for the people and who they were and, more importantly, you know, basically get the knowledge that they were peaceful and just a bunch of civilians that were really trying to move in stuff for their -- for the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So again we can conclude that you were informed about this from your conversations with those people. Could we now move into private session, please. Maybe we can check whether the following document is under seal. It's Prosecution document 02688. Could the registrar please check. If it's not under seal, we can remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: By you do not know what unit the Kinder platoon belonged to? When I say the Kinder platoon, I'm not talking about people whom you assume might be the Kinder platoon, but yesterday if you had not been told what those people were doing, you would never have arrived at that conclusion because you don't really know who or what the Kinder platoon was. You can only assume, conclude. But you don't have any first-hand information, and until yesterday you had not heard of the Kinder platoon. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but the Military Police Platoon is the one I have been referring to throughout my testimony, that I knew was active in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, we know that. You explained that yesterday. I just wanted to see what it was you did not know. You did not know what the Kinder platoon was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have concluded my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you remember, my name is Valentin Coric. I am an accused here in these proceedings. I will now use a document which we cannot show on the screen now, but I wish to tell you that you are not correct when yesterday you said, and this was suggested by the OTP, that the military police in Rama was in absolute control of the situation. Therefore, I ask you to be patient and answer my questions. But before that, I would like to read a report of the security and information service of the Rama Brigade. Have you heard of the SIS, the security and information service?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: In Rama did you ever ever come across Mr. Luka Markesic? Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that name. If you showed me a picture I might be able to identify him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to read this report. It's the only report I will use, and therefore I ask for the Court's indulgence. The heading is "Rama Prozor brigade, security and information service." The date is the 1st of June, 1993. The report is on events in the villages of Klek and Donji Krancici. "On the 27th of May, 1993, on the occasion of a conversation with ECMM monitors in the headquarters of the Rama Brigade, it transpired (information received from the imam from Prozor) that on the 26th of May, 1993, in the village of Klek an elderly man was murdered." I have now been told by my Defence team - I will interrupt reading this text - that this is P 02597. Could we please have it placed on the screen. I see that there's poor coordination in my team. So I'll continue to read and now you can follow. Do we have it on our screens? So: "On the 26th of May, 1993, in Klek one elderly man and two elderly women were killed and one girl was raped. After this information was received, the CIS of the Rama Brigade --" have you heard of CIS? I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, or have not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: SIS, rather, "security and information service came to conduct investigation. The officer of the SIS, Franjo, officer of the Rama Brigade SIS, who was sent there, and the doctor on duty, Dr. Sefik Hadzic," do you agree with me that this is a Muslim name, the name of the doctor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that because I'm not familiar with the -- what is a Muslim name and what is not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you might have learned in that time. "And established the following: "On the 26th of June, 1993, six soldiers in camouflage uniforms came to the village of Klek with the intention of looting. "These persons arrived in red-coloured vehicles and a grey Lada station-wagon, and on this occasion they killed," and now we can see the names that I'm not going to read, the names of the Muslims who were killed, and the person who was raped, to speed things up. "After that, the SIS of the Rama Brigade embarked upon a detailed investigation and took into custody the suspects." I underline this.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm confused again. In referring to page 1, we're talking about a date of 26 June, 1993, and now we jump to -- back and forth to another date of 27 May. Was this event even related, or is this two separate events? In the English translation I have June and then May, and then back to May. Sorry, it starts with May, goes to June, and then to May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I'm being told that this is an error in dates. The 25th of May -- I think these are two incidents. In one incident two persons were involved. In other incident six were involved. But if we read through, it will become clear.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on the 26th of June, that date is incorrect because the memo is written on the 1st of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: That's what the document says. I'm using a SIS document. This is not a police document. I am using what I have, but we'll see later where the problem lies. If you will bear with me, I would like to continue and then we'll deal with those issues. So when we are talking about this service that you never heard of, it seems to have taken these suspects into custody. Do you believe that the service did take these persons into custody, that their offices --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I believe and know are two different things. Unfortunately I cannot comment on whether they were or were not. I didn't see it happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's move on. "After initial interviews of the suspects, it was established that all three of them were involved in the crime together with another three members of the 1st Guard Brigade of the HVO who are on the run." So three were in custody, three on the run. "Then it was established that they were participants in another incident in Donji Krancici on the 27th of May, 1993, while the investigation for the previous incident was still under way. "These people came to Donji Krancici on the 27th of May, 1993, at around 2000 hours and began mistreating old men and children, looking for money and jewellery. They started confiscating motor vehicles and destroying the property of the rest accidents of the village, which is located in the liberated part of the municipality. "We emphasise that Muslims from that village go to the first front line facing the Chetniks. "The detained Jozo Glibo and Zoran Petkovic are being questioned by the Rama Brigade SIS, while the three so far unknown, unidentified members of the 1st Guards Brigade are on the run, while Pero Vidovic has been expelled to Croatia." Signed "SIS officer Franjo Krizanac." And this document was sent to the SIS of the operation zone north-west Herzegovina and the command of the Rama brigade. Therefore, can we conclude on the basis of this document that some other services to in Rama municipality and Rama town around Prozor were active? And I'm asking you whether you had any contacts with the Ministry of the Interior, MUP, and the police station in Rama. Okay. I understand you didn't have any contact with the SIS, but did you have any contact with the civilian military police in Rama?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have had contact with the civilian police, because if I remember correctly, it would have been collocated with the mayor of Prozor. I'm -- but to say, you know, that there was direct interaction about -- about these particular activities, first off I've got to openly admit that I don't even know where this place you're referring to in this document is in comparison to Prozor and whether it was even in my -- the area in which I resided. Gornji -- I'm sorry, I can't see the name, the second part of the down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Klek.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Prozor municipality, if I can be of assistance. So we're talking about villages in Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But obviously to the south of Prozor it became very vague as to our -- where -- where our line was drawn. To say that it was further south than where I was able to get access would tell you that I would probably have limited or no knowledge of this occurring.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: But I should like to come back to this report that I'm dealing with today, the only one, to read to you the first sentence. "On the 27th of May, 1993, in talking with ECM monitors." So I'm asking you how is it possible? Those were your men. On the 1st of June you were on duty, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But once again, I must emphasise that it could have been any number of ECM monitors in that location that they may have talked to. Whether it was specifically me, I cannot answer that unless I had my report to refer to on that day. Remembering that, you know, 1st of June is kind of my first sort of getting my feet wet in that area, and to say that I had actual contact with the SIS, I cannot give you that. It may be my partner. It may have been the -- another team from another location, and I can give you no more than that. Unless you specifically identify where this occurred, how it occurred, I can't further comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you mean to say that in your area, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf and Rama, other teams were able to come and do your job? Were they coming with your approval, or did they come without any notification or announcement?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else did my job. The situation is that I remind you that the "road to salvation" moved through Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. ECMM monitors moved up and down through our area quite often, and we in fact would inter -- we would interact with these -- with these individuals as they moved through and did their work. Our AOR, area of responsibility, included three communities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Colonel. A moment ago, in your previous answer, you said that maybe another team talked to SIS officers, officers of the service you never heard of. That's what you said. Could any passerby, just anybody from the European monitoring team just walk up to any member of the brigade and talk to them. Does that sound logical to you? Could you comment?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activity -- it would -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate a brief answer. I don't have time. The Judges are already looking askance at me. You can't have it both ways. It's -- you have to give up one of these possibilities. Let me just remind you that the day before you went to Rama to have a meeting and now you are testifying in The Hague about killings, about rapes that are really documented, that really did happen, that people are being tried for or have been tried for. So where are we? What is the position? The day after that meeting you have no information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, you are here to ask questions, and maybe it would be a good idea if you let the witness answer. He started to answer, you interrupt him. He starts again, you interrupt him. We are interested in what the witness has to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel. Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is to doubt about my area of responsibility and who played in my area. In fact, I used to -- in fact, I got very upset when individuals, and I'm referring to other agencies, would come into my area and play without me knowing about it. The ECMM, the way it was set up, allowed us to operate independently within our areas of responsibility. The issue was that teams would move through our area, through our area, as a stop point on its way into Zenica. Now, if you're asking me is the possibility that an individual would be -- an ECM monitor would be stopped and talked to by an individual of the SIS, then it is possible. Whether to say it was me I cannot answer that, because first of all, I do not know or understand where this town is you're referring to. If I had that, then I can give you a sort of general answer to say, yes, it probably was me. If it is in an area very much south of Prozor, then you're running into Mike 2, which is a different ECMM responsibility, and they may have had contact with the SIS. That's what I'm trying to refer to. There is no doubt what was happening in my area. I knew what was going on. And nobody played in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Colonel, when you speak south of Prozor, do you have the limits of the municipality in mind for the location of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have the defined location between Mike 2 and ourself. I have no idea what the limit -- sitting here right now, what the limit of the Prozor municipality is. All I know is the distance is halfway between Mostar and ourselves in Prozor, that major road was divided, and everything to the north was mine and everything to the south happened to belong to Mike 2, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be possible to show you a map where the town is indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Then I could help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could the usher do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this isn't helping me much either. You're going to have to orient me. I see Prozor in the centre here, and the town that you're referring to is located where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is Klek, and it is located 4.00, the direction 4.00. There is a square around it. It's marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the top of my pen right now; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Donji Krancici is just a little way above. May I continue? I have only two more brief questions and we'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: So you met up with General Praljak in some sort of restaurant didn't you. But this meeting on the 27th of May was held in the command headquarters of the Rama Brigade, not just anyplace. That's what this document says, if we go back to page 1. Is that what's written? So, Colonel, my last question: Does this document demonstrate, and not only this one but a series of other documents, that your information as representatives and monitors of the European Monitors was indeed reacted to by the HVO? They went to the scene, took the suspects and the perpetrators into custody and started questioning them. The offences involved were very serious. And I'm not questioning your contribution. It is indeed very valuable that you provided the information but would you agree that this is the case?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one incident which occured on the 27th of May, 1993. It does not address the situation which happened in July and August.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one incident which was dealt with. It appeared to have been dealt with by -- by the -- by the HVO. Of which I may not even have knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Colonel, as you formed your opinions that you presented yesterday, I could say by the same token, if the Trial Chamber allows me, that I can produce another 40 documents that were developed during your mandate, and I could tender them. But most of these documents have already been exhibited, and they will be dealt with when we come to the last stages of the Defence case. I have no further questions. Thank you, Colonel. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 10 minutes left. I can see that three Defence counsel have not taken the floor. Mr. Ibrisimovic, Ms. Nozica, Mr. Karnavas. So what is it to be? Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have already given up our time in favour of other Defence teams and we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'll try to be brief. I don't know if I'll be able to finish within the allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir -- Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First I just want to -- some housekeeping matters. Going back to your testimony, the first time that you were here testifying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you testified the first time in the previous case on 18 May, 2004, there was a question posed to you and you were asked about some specific names and you said that you could not provide these names unless you referred to notes. That would be on page 7598 of the -- of the transcript in the previous case, which would be the Hadzihasanovic on 18 May, 2004. My question is: When you testified in that case, did you have notes or were you referring to the reports that -- that you had generated?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the reports, and I continue to refer back to the reports because they are the concrete written record of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now, Colonel, when you were prepared for that case by the Office of the Prosecution, did they actually show you your reports? Were they available for you to look at and refer to in order to refresh your memory? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the detail that we have here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you came to The Hague, before and prior to giving -- to give your evidence yesterday, I suspect that you met with the Prosecutor, the gentleman who has been questioning you. Were all of your reports made available to you at that point in time or just the report -- the reports that you generated and others generated for the purposes of introducing into evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was made available to me was my previous statements and these reports here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so I take it from your answer that there are other reports that you generated that were not made available to you, and that's what you've been referring to for the last couple days, if you could refer to your reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you did not make copies of your own reports for your own archive?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, I have a couple of questions with regard to your statements. You gave two statements, and I find it rather curious. Nothing to do with you, by the way, but just curious in the sense that the first statement that you gave was on 9th and 10th October, 2001. You were interviewed by a gentleman by the name of Brett Pakenham. Now, sir, if I may ask, were you interviewed in Canada at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you interviewed in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you were in theatre someplace?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm not trying to pry into exactly where you were. So they actually had to come and get you to take your statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The second time was a month later and that was on the 28th and 29th of November, 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you in the same location or had you moved back home or --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I find it rather curious is as follows, and perhaps this is more for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, is that on the first statement that you give, you're asked questions that are exclusively against the Croats, and a month later, when you're questioned by another interview, Tom Parker, it would appear the same period, the same events, you're only asked questions that would be against the Muslims. Would that be a fair assessment, first of all?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it you were not conducting -- you were not directing the flow of the interview. You were being asked questions and you were answering the questions to the best of your ability; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was asked to give a statement as to what I felt had transpired between certain dates on which I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I was inarticulate in that question. All right. You were asked the questions and you provided the answers; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I find it rather interesting that if you are in theatre, as you were, working as a monitor, being a soldier and officer and having spent at -- been on five different missions as I understand it, you would -- you would agree with me, would you not, that in order to understand a particular event or set of events one would have to look at these events in context, would they not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, we just can't take an isolated incident, isolate it to one side and try to make sense of it without looking at all of the events; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again getting back to my earlier question, you were not the one that had chosen to conduct these particular interviews in this fashion, in other words, one for the Muslims and one for the Croats. That was something that the Office of the Prosecution decided to do on its own for reasons perhaps that were made available to you or not?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll clarify that a lot of the interviews were conducted based on location and where things had happened rather than a specific ethnic group, and that's what we explored throughout the interview process. So, you know, there were -- in both interviews both sides came up on certain situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, the reason I'm asking is I find it rather curious, because I can tell you that in my jurisdiction, in the United States, anywhere, whether it's state or federal, I expect it's the same in Canada, no investigator would do it in this fashion. They would try to get one complete statement from the individual, perhaps go back for clarification purposes. I'm perhaps wondering why would the Prosecution in this case send investigators on two different occasions to far places to get interviews on matters of context?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it a question to the witness about the actions of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you question -- did you question the methodology, why would they want to take these events out of context? Because it would seem to me for instance if we wanted to understand what was happening in your zone of operation or area of operation throughout that entire period we would have to take you chronologically and get a chronological narrative, as it were. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that when I was initially contacted, it wasn't by one side and then the other side. It was -- I was contacted over the events that I had experienced over a period of time which then two individuals came down and interviewed me specifically about areas in the north and areas in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's how we came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were there other matters, because I just to ask this last question, were there other the matters regarding your tenure which you were not asked to give clarification on because I find it rather interesting that one fellow would come in from the north, one from the south. Did anybody come from the center, east, west, north, south? It just doesn't make sense to me. So did they -- were there areas, were there gaps in your statement because they, being the Office of the Prosecution, failed to ask about particular incidents that might perhaps be necessary that information that is in order to put entire events into context and at least well on your watch?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to project openly, and I have no favour against one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. That's very clear. That's very clear.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the issue that there were many incidents that had occurred in a very, very short time frame of which I was witness to, and I tried to project and give that information as openly as I could and not, once again, trying to steer it in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's very obvious, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know we're out of time. I have approximately 10 minutes for tomorrow, 15 at the very maximum, but I think I can keep it under 10 minutes. There are just some minor points I need to touch on. And might I add I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You only need 10 minutes. Mrs. Nozica, do you wish to put some questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have questions, and I would like to use up the time allocated to us in the beginning, 30 minutes. Maybe I will finish sooner but I would like not to promise that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would add that looking at the following three witnesses, Your Honour, three witnesses for the rest of the week, unless something unusual happens we do not intend to ask any questions, so that would not interfere with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, I'm sure you've understood the Defence counsel still has 40 minutes. Can you stay until tomorrow? Is that a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a problem, unfortunately, Your Honour. I have other national obligations in a place far away from here or not too far away from here which I must take part in tomorrow morning, and I have no problem about continuing today for the total amount of time you need me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we will have to continue. We will have a 10- to 15-minute break now, and then we shall resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The session continues. Before I give the floor to the Defence, I apologise to the interpreters for this extension. We will be working an hour longer. I draw the attention of the Defence to the following: As I have already said, when putting questions, put questions about the most important points, the essential points relating to what is in the indictment. Paragraphs 52, 53, 54, 55, are concerned with Prozor. This morning we spent nearly two hours discussing convoys. Convoys are not mentioned in these counts of the indictment. They are a separate issue. There are fundamental issues which were not raised at all, and yet you should have cross-examined the witness on them. The result of all this is that you are not succeeding in completing your cross-examination in the time set. We therefore have to extend our sessions. Therefore, from now on we will have to be far stricter in the time we grant you. From now on, before every session we have to say that each accused has only so much time, and when that time expires we will take the floor from you. We now have an hour ahead of us. The witness must finish his testimony today. He is unable to return tomorrow morning. I now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, who needs only a few minutes, if I'm not mistaken. I wish to ask him not to put any questions about convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, there was one question only because there's a document that the gentleman refers to, but if you wish for me not to, I won't. But thank you, and of course we can always use guidance from the Bench on asking the most relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you had indicated that the situation changed quite dramatically while you were there, particularly after -- or while you were on vacation, on leave, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess I want to focus a little bit on that aspect of it, because it was when you returned that obviously there was a push from north to south, correct, by the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at one point, as I recall your testimony yesterday, in essence there was a large number of -- of Croats that were more or less sandwiched into an area; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think the figure is somewhere around 10.000 to 15.000. Now, sir, you indicated that at some point those folks went, I guess it would be east -- no, west, west, and then north -- and then south. I'm sorry. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when they went west they would have gone into Serb-held territory in order to go down south where -- where the Croats were still there at that point in time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I looked at the transcript last night, but I thought I heard you use the word that they escaped or were escaping. Some -- a word to that effect. Did I hear you correctly, that in essence, given the situation, you could tell us, in light of what was happening with the battle going on, would it be fair to say that in light of where they were, in essence, they had to escape that area in order to get -- to seek sanctuary in a sense?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, and what I'm trying to drive at is this was not something that they did on their own volition in the sense that, okay, let's leave the area so we can occupy another area. Because of the circumstances, they being civilians in the middle of two warring factions, they had to get out the way; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say between two warring factions. One of the warring factions was the one that was sandwiched between the other, and I believe everybody left, including soldiers. It was one of survival, because they knew that things were going to happen. And while I was in that pocket I also was present when -- when action -- actions were taken and they were being fired upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we could say this was an act of necessity on their part?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both civilian and soldiers, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I understand it, at that point in time the UNHCR had sort of a different policy or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, please. The question that Mr. Karnavas is asking you is a very important question, and it's the kind of question the Trial Chamber likes to hear. Those refugees, you say that among them there were civilians and soldiers alike, that they set out together. We on the Bench are interested in the following: Did the civilians set out first followed by the soldiers or did the soldiers leave their positions due to offensive actions of the other side, and did that then result in the movement of the civilian population? What would be your analysis of the situation? Was it a movement of general panic, civilians and troops leaving at the same time, or was it a movement that -- in which we can distinguish various times of departure, first civilians, followed by troops, or the other way round? If you could clarify the situation, please. And that is the type of question that is very useful indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came upon -- we were actually -- got word that it was a mixture of both civilian and military. And when we did come upon the situation, it was -- everybody was mixed in, everybody.
