Realising that the call was made to rescue, and I use that word wisely, to rescue injured who were trapped, we were given and had use of the battle bus, I refer to the Croat battle bus, of which was armoured, armed as in plating, armoured plating around the outside of the bus, and we were able to use that with my vehicle and Warrior to go into this location to "take out the injured." When we arrived, there was panic, and to the point where men, women, and children were attempting to hijack the bus to get out of there, and my partner was forced to use physical force in order to remove people. At the same time, we are trying to move injured from the casualty collection point in a small house onto the bus, while at the same time we came under mortar fire and the situation worsened. The Brit company, one of its platoons was with me in close protection went hatches down, yellow and myself, hit the dirt along a rock fence and we sat out the situation in a very surreal situation of which complete panic and disarray while we were sitting there having a cigarette, literally. The situation finally simmered down. We loaded who we could and we took off down towards Prozor to drop off the injured. It was that night then when we went back and found that everybody was gone and I'm referring to soldiers, women, children, and men not in uniform. It was at that time that we had discovered that they had moved. I would also like to bring to your attention that buildings were burned on their way out and things were placed on fire. In fact, even the HVO headquarters in Prozor was torched prior to their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course if they had to escape on short notice and they had documents that might be secret -- of secret nature, maps and what have you, one would understand why such a thing would occur, would it not? At least the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular headquarters was torched the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, but the situation, sir, on the ground as it was unfolding was rather rapid, rather panicking, and it was rather evident that they were going to have to evacuate the area or leave the area?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I guess I want to focus a little bit on the UNHCR. To what extent was the UNHCR providing assistance at this point in time to protect these -- these non-combatants, the non-combatants at least to make sure they didn't have to leave their areas?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that was in the mandate of the UNHCR to protect anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you. I'm just asking if you saw anybody, because the reason I'm asking that question is UNHCR, as I understand, had a particular policy at the time that the displaced persons or refugees should be kept where they are and not be moved or the -- the civilians not be moved. And so if that's the UNHCR position, one would presume that the UNHCR, being a United Nations organisation, coming up with such a policy under these circumstances would obviously be providing comfort and safety to those individuals.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I -- I honestly cannot sit here and state that UNHCR was even active in my area. I cannot remember meeting with the UNHCR representative other than later on when things started to get disconnected and we ended up meeting with representation of one-off, one individual showing up and then discussions started to happen up north with Father Janko, who is the priest in Bugojno and so on and so forth, and that's when we started interacting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you interacting with the UNHCR Zenica office or UNHCR Mostar office if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have logically been the Zenica office more than the Mostar office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you remember if they strongly recommended not to remove the DPs from the area in order to avoid mass movements of population?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was an UNHCR policy or not I'm not sure, but you can understand the dichotomy that one ends up in. If ethnic cleansing is taking place and you are in a position to remove people, are you not achieving what they want to do? In other words, if -- if the population is being pushed by one side to move and then you jump in there to save the day and then move them, is that not what they tried to achieve? Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That makes some sense. Of course, the alternative is if you're not trying to assist them in moving out of harm's way, one would expect the folks in Geneva and New York and where have you would provide the necessary wherewithal to make sure that they would protect those people. So either the UNHCR would come up with the military or maybe the UNPROFOR would be there to protect. So you being on the ground it was either UNHCR or UNPROFOR capable, able, willing, and did they in fact provide the necessary assistance in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm against this line of cross-examination. What is the point of this cross-examination? Is it emanating from examination-in-chief? It does not. Is Mr. Karnavas contesting the witness's credibility? He is not. What is the relevance of these questions with respect to UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- well, the gentleman was absent last week. Perhaps if he had been with us in other sessions it might be relevant, but one of the key issues that's in the indictment and that the Prosecution continues to advocate is that this was a form of self-cleansing, that the Croats were cleansing themselves out of certain areas in order to create a homogenous pocket, and here we have a gentleman on the ground and he's telling us exactly that they had to escape, that some had to be rescued. Contrary to -- to certain allegations that the HZ HB was trying to self-cleanse certain areas. That's the purpose. And my line of questioning was if the UNHCR or other UN agencies have such a policy, are promoting a policy not to move populations, and I agree with the gentleman with respect to ethnic cleansing, but if you find yourself in a situation where a civilian population, large numbers, 10.000, 15.000, are trapped and you have this very rigid policy, one would expect the UNHCR to step up to the plate with their army or to use the UNPROFOR. So were you able to do that? Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry. Is it statement by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a question. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And a very long one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've heard the question. It was a lengthy question. Do you have anything to contribute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing that I would make a comment on is reaction time. The situation, of course, was not good in those days, and you had to make the call on the day as to what sort of reaction you had to do and carry on. To call on the cavalry of the UNHCR or a bigger UNPROFOR would not have happened. We had the resources we had. I cannot comment on UNHCR policy or UN policy. I was ECMM at the time and which I carried out my mission to the best of my ability, one team, one place, with many different problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you say "we", earlier in your answer, was that "we" ECMM or we UNPROFOR or collectively the internationals that were there to make sense of --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I would make -- I would stand and state that "we" is the collective here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I listened to you very carefully and you seem to choose your words very carefully and you seem to be a careful individual, and you made a point of telling us repeatedly that it was not within your responsibility. I take it you were very concerned about what is common referred to as mission creep, taking on more responsibility than your mission calls -- calls for or your mandate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me if I saw situations unfold which I then morally put them up against that sort of criteria, I did something about it, yes, I did, and if you want to call that mission creep, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think you misunderstood my -- my question. Repeatedly you've been asked about information. For instance, do you know, you know, how many soldiers were there, who they were and what have you, and occasionally you would tell us that was not within my responsibility. I was not there to count heads. I was not there looking at maps and what have you. I take it you stuck to your, narrow as it was, one primarily because it was rather narrow too. You were walking around in a white uniform, unarmed, and being a professional soldier and having been in theatre before, you know how dangerous it can be if you just start, you know, acting up without the cavalry behind you; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And the resources that we had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said yesterday that you were collocated with the BritBats that were there, and I happen to know that the Canadian Armed Forces have a relatively good if not very good relationship with the UK armed forces. They do training together and what have you. And I take it, while you were being collocated and exchanging information, perhaps you became aware of what is commonly referred to as the rules of engagement for UNPROFOR. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state that I did not read their rules of engagement. I understood what the rules of engagement were, realising that they were armed, had tracked vehicles and had firepower to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us a little bit what their rules of engagement were? I mean, what exactly could they do? I know if shot upon they could shoot back.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Barring that, however, they were not supposed to take sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we saw that in Srebrenica, in fact. But that was much later. But nonetheless, what about for the protection of civilians? Were they -- was it within their mandate, within their rules of engagement, if it comes within their rules of engagement, to, for instance, create a buffer zone between the civilians and a particular warring faction that is on the attack, on the offensive, trying to drive these people out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite struck by what you said when you mentioned the refugees. You explained that you were there, that UNPROFOR was there, and that there was mortar fire, and the mortar fire was also firing at the civilian population. In a case like that, if it were a case of legitimate defence, could UNPROFOR hit back and fire back if there was mortar fire, because the mortar fire was landing on the civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mortar fire or any sort of indirect fire is indiscriminate as to where it lands. You can get it within a grid square. I overexaggerate. But if it's fired in your general direction it's going to start to impact in and around you. The immediate reaction of UNPROFOR in that particular circumstance was to go to ground, and that is the likelihood of a round actually hitting an armoured vehicle is limited to none but it would experience shrapnel, and therefore as a result of that you tend to take a very defensive mode. Unfortunately, the company was not equipped with any anti-mortar capability, i.e., detection and/or counter battery fire. So it had to make do with the resources that it had, and it was the only Warrior with the 30-millimetre gun. So to say the mortar round came from point X and fired at point X could not be achieved with the resources that were there. So it was just a matter to get people to cover and more importantly UNPROFOR itself to get to cover. That's the indirect role. Obviously in the direct role you're able to determine very quickly where rounds are coming from, and I would suggest that it would -- UNPROFOR would have the wherewithal to return fire in that particular case if it was direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess I just want to make sure that -- that I establish this point. Going back to Bugojno, obviously you have a push or an advancement by the army of BiH. Do you know whether UNPROFOR at that point in time could of sort of got in between as a buffer, a buffer between the army of BiH and say the HVO and the civilians in order to stop the advancement of the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Realising that when the offensive started to happen, I was in fact not in location. Realising the size of the -- of the -- of the action, a company would not have been sufficient, especially in the area of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I believe I read somewhere that you mentioned that at one point you saw some Mujahedin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Where did you see them if your recollection serves you well?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recall about what time -- what period would that have been?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the period of time of the action that we're referring to in the August time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Trial Chamber feel that the questions put during the examination-in-chief did not concern the Mujahedin, so there's no particular reason for putting these questions to the witness. Why do you want him to testify and to tell you that he has seen Mujahedins in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's a very common rule of evidence in trial advocacy, yes, Judge Trechsel, because you seem astonished at what I'm about to say, and that is that simply because a question isn't raised on direct examination, on cross, if it's relevant to the Defence case, I can certainly go into it. It is relevant for a couple of reasons. One, because we have heard testimony even from a previous member of the ECMM that the mere mentioning of the Mujahedin would cause people to run in any particular free direction and that even the Muslims, Bosniaks themselves were afraid of these foreign fighters. It is relevant again going back to why would these people flee the area. So I think it's relevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to the Mujahedin, if you could tell us, did you approach them in your capacity to find out who they were, what were they doing, who is their commander?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only observed them in the town of Bugojno in groups that would be moving around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I don't want to put you on the spot, but is there a particular reason why you didn't -- I don't want to say confront them but ask them like who are you, what are you doing over here, or was that beyond your mandate?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dealt at -- I did not deal at the individual soldier level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than those I was confronted with on a particular road crossing or -- or checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In light of that answer, can I assume that at some point you might have approached the ABiH commander or local commander to find out under whose command these people were or is this something that didn't alarm you at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were under command, I would suggest that I did ask that question. Are Mujahedin in the area? And the response would have been yes. Now, to what size I cannot comment whether it was battalion or individuals -- individuals fighting alongside particular units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that before you got into theatre, into this particular area, the Gornji Vakuf area, you had stopped in Zenica for some -- I don't want to say training but some -- to be briefed, being correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mission specific training or briefings which basically gives you the lay of the land that you're walking into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. At that at that point in time did they by any chance inform you about the presence of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this was your first opportunity to come across and --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was to my surprise that they were there. We had heard indications that they were operating in the southern portion down near Mostar, but we had not seen anything in our area until that August time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last question on that. How did you know that they were Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By their dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And their appearance, beards and what have you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beards, tend to be in a karkeet [phoen] coloured clothing consisting -- and there's probably a legitimate name for it, but consisting of a long top shirt, went down to the knees, a hat round, placed upon the head, and bandoliers normally strung across the front with a vest of some sort and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So they stuck out?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sure did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you had asked for 10 minutes. We are already up to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one last question. It's not about convoys. I scrapped that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This has to do with the Muslim refugees in Prozor. You told us that at least we saw one particular report that as early as 1992 a large number of refugees, Muslim refugees, had made it to Prozor as they were being pushed out by the Bosnian Serb army. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that report that we referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall -- do you know how many of those refugees were still in Prozor or that particular time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know whether the folks that you saw that you said they were there at the outskirts of the town and then one day they were sort of -- they left and you caught up with the last truck, I believe, do you know whether they were part of that refugee movement or were they actually residents of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These individuals were -- I would assume were individuals that had been gathered over a long period of time, and it could have been a mixture of people from the Prozor region or from any other region. There was a grouping of about 1.500 people, if I remember correctly, all Muslim background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, I -- thank you, sir. Thank you very, very much for coming here and giving your evidence. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I will put a few brief questions to you so we can proceed very quickly. Yesterday, in your responses during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned the torching of houses in certain villages. This was when you were shown a document, and I would like to have it on e-court. I don't know if you still have your bundle of documents before you. Could we please see P 02817 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I can't see e-court. You have it. I don't know whether the others in the courtroom can see it, but I will proceed. First, on page 1, can we establish that this is a report of the 17th of June, 1993? Is that correct? And perhaps we can have page 7 in e-court, which was shown to you by the Prosecutor. As I cannot see anything on my screen, could you please look at the part where it says "Gornji Vakuf, Prozor 2." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 7, what paragraph, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, V2." That's what the first few words are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: We don't have connections, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In English it's on page 5. It begins with the words "Gornji Vakuf". Now, it seems we all have it, yes. Now we have that part in e-court. If you could please take a look. The third paragraph. It says "V2 attended a joint patrol with UNPROFOR east of route Diamond."

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this part yesterday, when responding to a question by the Prosecutor, and this starts on page 83, line 23 and goes on until page 25, line 6, you said that in your opinion the burning of those houses in those villages, Stipici, and you also mentioned the village of Rat, both are mentioned here, you said that in your opinion it was members of the HVO that torched the houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but -- but may I bring your attention that the houses that were burning at the time were houses that were on the way to these locations, remembering that these three towns are up in the hills. And the burnings that I witnessed on that particular day were on the main route, Route Diamond, towards Gornji Vakuf and up towards Zenica. It was the houses on the left and right of the road that were being torched, not in the exact towns of Srebrenica and -- or sorry, and the three towns that are stated there, which includes Rat.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you at any time -- well, it doesn't say here who torched the houses, but did you ever go to the villages of Rat and Stipici and see people taking property out of these houses on the Sunday after the 11th of June, and did you see who was taking property out of the houses and possibly torching them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two separate visits up to this location I remember. The initial one was fairly quiet, and we were just going up into that area to talk to people. The second one was this situation where we started seeing the burning happening. And the third that comes to mind is the extraction or the removing of those people from this area. And they were all brought to the southern-most community, which was a perpendicular road to the -- to the road that led from Gornji Vakuf up to -- up to Zenica, and this was the place that I was talking about where buses were organised by the Croats to evacuate people out of these communities of which I was witness to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the village of Rat and in the village of Stipici and around these villages, on both of these visits, did you ever see soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina taking things out of the houses? And when you looked back, did you see them torching houses, and did you possibly discuss this with members of the army of BH and inform the regional centre in Zenica about it? And we are talking about June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the foundation for this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The foundation for this question is the Prosecutor's question of yesterday as to who was torching the houses in the period in question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are asking me whether I had witnessed others doing this particular act, then the answer has to be yes, and not necessarily in that location. There were many burnings of many houses, including blowing them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. We may proceed. My colleague Mr. Karnavas put a question to you, and you replied that you had indeed made a statement on the 28th of November, 2001, and as I feel that everything that happened in Bugojno and in the area is extremely important for the Defence, since these events spilled over into the events mentioned in the indictment, would the usher please give the witness his statement of the 28th of November, 2001. And for Your Honours, I have put the English version in the file. I am referring to page 4, paragraph 2, and let us see what the witness stated about this on the 28th of November, 2001. Above this the date is the 11th of June, 1993. Let me remind you that in the report when you mentioned the villages the date is the 17th of June. However, I'm referring to the following paragraph: "For the next week, we joined BritBat on patrols of the wider area visiting some of the more remote villages and trying to get a feel for how far the fighting had spread after the trouble in Travnik. We made a couple of trips up to the villages of Rat and Stipici. On the second visit I remember driving past a small group of ABiH soldiers emptying a house in Stipici of furniture. I didn't think anything was particularly untoward - they didn't look especially concerned to see us - and I assumed they were probably just salvaging their own property. However, when we reached Rat and looked back down the road, we saw that all the houses where the soldiers had been working were now on fire. I made a note in my daily report to RC Zenica to the effect that the armija was practising ethnic cleansing in Stipici." Is this what it says? Well, there's no doubt that's what it says, but has this refreshed your memory, and do you now perhaps remember this event, and is it the same event described in the report? And let me stress that the report is dated on the 17th. So this is the same time period. Could you say something about this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think logically if you read through my initial statement, it kind of moves from the 11th of June to the 18th, so I would assume that it is around the same time frame, that is correct. Did you want me to make further comment on this or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. What you said yesterday, that it was HVO soldiers torching these houses, is not consistent with what it says here, that it was army of Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers who were doing that. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that the events happened some 13 years ago plus a statement of 2001 and plus my recollection of yesterday, maybe misinterpreted by time. I put that forward and would make the recommendation that on one side of the road one events were happening, other side of the road other events were happening, and we're trying to -- in any recollection, trying to make it a clear delineation as to who was doing what to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, follow-up question. Yesterday you were very clear, and according to what you said, these were soldiers, HVO soldiers that set fire to the houses. In the written statement, there are ABiH soldiers who are setting fire to the buildings. Perhaps there's some confusion in your mind over this. Do you remember having seen HVO soldiers set fire to these houses? Perhaps this wasn't in Stipici. Perhaps it was elsewhere. Perhaps there is some confusion in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may well be confusion. Over time my mind does get a little bit grey. Unfortunately, I can openly state that I witnessed both sides doing this action. And now whether this -- I confused two different dates, that maybe the case, but I can also give you other specific times where there is no doubt that it was HVO that was doing it, if we want to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the other hand, you can't tell us in which places you saw HVO soldiers setting fire to some of the houses, and you can't give us a date either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you a -- I can give you that there -- that they were setting fire between the area of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. I can also give you the fact that houses were blown up right outside our camp on many -- or during many evenings or during the middle of the night by the HVO rolling mines from the high feature to the south into occupied houses and which would eliminate -- any one mine would eliminate five houses, and we would pick up the pieces the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are quite positive, and you give us an example because you were next door you said that the HVO were rolling mines from the top of the hill and that these mines, when they hit the houses, the -- some of the houses were blown up. I think you mentioned five of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now take a look at the following. Yesterday, on pages 58 from line 10 to page 59, line 24, you spoke about the exhumation of soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you happened to come upon. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When the citizens were gathered there said that they had been tortured, and yesterday in the course of your testimony you said that you were unable to establish anything except that they were shot. Do you remember who it was who was exhuming these people, digging them up?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was civilians that were digging them up. They were surrounded by civilian police, I believe from the Bugojno area. There was a doctor there, if I remember correctly. There was ambulance service in order to take the bodies away. Once again, we came down the road and looked to our right and there's large gathering of people, and people were trying to summon us over to take a look at what had transpired.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were there Croat prisoners of war there?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. And I'm glad you reminded me of that one. The -- there were Croats that were actually doing the digging, if I remember correctly. They were the ones that were being tasked to dig up the bodies, if I remember correctly. And you would probably find it in my statement someplace. That was the thing -- kind of thing that stuck out at me, because they were surrounded by people with -- with rifles, and they were down actually doing the digging.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I did find it in your report on page -- pages 7 and 8, but since you remember it, we won't dwell on it any longer. In your statement, you said that they dug up three Muslims. Yesterday you said four, but you weren't sure of the exact number. Would it then be logical to conclude that what you stated in your previous statement is correct, because you say explicitly they were digging up the grave of three Muslims? Take a look at your statement if you like.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm missing -- was a misinterpretation as to who the soldiers were who were dead or -- I'm not sure what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. Yesterday, you said that the number of Muslims dug up was four, whereas in this statement you said it was three. So I think it's quite important to establish how many there were.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Understood. Once again, things fade with time. What is said in the statement could be put up against the daily report would actually reflect the exact amount. And on going off the top of my head, four is stuck in my mind. If it was three and it's stated in here a such, then it was likely three.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now dwell on the situation in Bugojno briefly in the time period we are talking about now. Did you visit any prisons in Bugojno where Croats were detained at the time? Just very briefly what prisons did you visit? How many imprisoned Croats there were in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over time I had visited three locations. They had been either gathered, moved, and eventually moved on to another location. And the total number, I want to guesstimate, probably just under 500 when you add them all up, and that is a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did Father Janko tell you anything about the crimes committed against Croats at that time, and did he give you any documents or lists confirming what he said?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And those lists were -- and that's what we were talking about earlier, about our interaction with UNHCR, and we passed those lists accordingly, and I spent almost a full day with Father Janko in order to gather this information. And for the lack of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I don't know whether the name mentioned here should be mentioned. I don't know if this person benefits from any protective measures. I shall ask the registrar to make sure that this is taken off the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if it has to be redacted, I can't tell you exactly where, but during Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination the name was also mentioned. That's why I felt I could mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you want to add anything, sir? Excuse me. I see that your reply was interrupted, so would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just during that time that all formal structure of civilian authority or military had disappeared on -- in the area of Bugojno on behalf of the Croats. So the void was filled by the church and Father Janko. So those that had remained behind tended to be drawn to the church as a mechanism in which to bring forward as much information as they could on particular events, and that's how we ended up interacting with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my last topic. Yesterday, you mentioned the imam from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We have to change the tapes round so we have to make a very short break. So we have to count up to 10 and then we can start again. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned the imam from Prozor several times. In any conversations in Prozor, did you learn anything about his previous activities in arming the Muslim army? And I'm using this expression on purpose. You will see why.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- when you do follow on there is more to this which is of concern to me in that the imam basically took on the function very similar to that of Father Janko except in opposite communities and opposite situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I appreciate this, but I have very little time left, so I'm asking you a very specific, particular question. We are talking about holy people, and I'm now referring to the arming of any side. So did you have any information to this effect about the imam? I know what the role of these people was in these communities, especially in times of war, but my question is very specific.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge whatsoever the imam was involved in any sort of arming of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we have placed on the ELMO, and I do apologise to the Court, I only found these documents last night, I have not translated them, I will read them very briefly, but if we could put document 2D 00185 on the ELMO. They are two brief documents. And then I will ask the usher to stay by the ELMO, and then we shall look at 184, and then we'll put a question to the witness. Would it assist you if I were to tell you that his name was Elkaz Hidajet, the name of the imam?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we look at document 2D 00185 on the ELMO. Yes, this is it. Yes. I will read it out slowly. In the heading it says: "The chief imam of the committee of the Islamic Community in Prozor. Elkaz Hidajet Efendi in Prozor the 4th of September, 1992. The title is the Kuwait Igasa, Split office, esteemed brothers and there follows something in Arabic. On Monday, the 31st of August, 1992, I was in your office in Split accompanied by Salih Efendi Colakovic for talks on arming Muslim fighters on the territory of Prozor municipality. We have been promised help by the representative of the Kuwait Igasa in light infantry weapons and we were also asked to deliver a specific list of the necessary weapons and ammunition verified by the stamp of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "Enclosed with this letter please find the requested list properly verified. Please help us as soon as possible and meet our request. We also ask you to explain to the person bringing this letter and this order when and where we can take delivery of the requested weapons and ammunition. We also wish to inform you that I was -- I have been prevented by my regular duties from delivering this order to you in person, and I hope you will take this into account. Finally, I wish to thank you for your assistance, and may Djalla Shannuh reward you with djanet. Chief imam, Elkaz Hidajet," and there follows the stamp of the Islamic Community. Were you aware of the fact that this humanitarian organisation called Igasa was active in Croatia and that this was in fact a humanitarian organisation, a Muslim humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware. And this is from 1992, well before my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I know it's before your time. I was just trying to establish whether this was the same person, because more than once you mentioned that this person's communications were somehow limited. So I'm just trying to check whether this is the same person. And to round this off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Can the Defence counsel tell us where she got the document from in this particular format? Which archives did you turn to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not from the archives. This is a document found by the Defence. We will not tender it into evidence. We are simply showing it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you can't tell us where this document comes from. This could be a forgery, a forged document. You want to get across the fact that the imam in Prozor played a role in arming the Muslims. So that's your theory. Seemingly, this is what this document demonstrates, but we would like to know where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was collected by the investigators of Mr. Stojic. We have here the signature of the gentleman. And this will not be the only document speaking to these activities. If there is any doubt, we shall call an expert to examine the document. However, as I said, I am not tendering it into evidence. I'm only showing it. We will tender it when we have all the elements that will enable us to do so. Could we please have placed on the ELMO 2D 00184, which is the order or the list mentioned by the imam from Prozor, and it's signed by commander captain Muharem Sabic. And it says: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Prozor, registration number, date 2nd of September, 1992". It's addressed to the Kuwait Igasa, to the office in Split, and the subject is request for assistance in arming the Muslim fighters of Prozor, and it says: "Please deliver to us the following quantities of weapons and ammunition which will be used for us in the defence and liberation of our home. "200 piece of automatic rifles. "50 pieces of light machine-guns. "80 Zolja rocket launchers, and "250.000 -- 250.000 bullets, 7.62 millimetres in calibre." I wanted to ask the witness in connection with this imam, whether from his communications with the imam, he was aware that he was one of the organisers of the arming and equipping of, as he says, the Muslim army while you would call it the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware. My exposure to him was himself, his wife, and his -- his children in the town of Prozor. When I arrived in that location, that's the only exposure that I had to him from the point of view of me visiting him in his home on a daily basis as much as I could based on the situation. But I was unaware of this happening in the background and, more importantly, from the 1991 time frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 1992. Thank you. That's all. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If there are no further questions. There's no re-examination. In any case, we would not have any time. Colonel, thank you for coming to The Hague. We have extended the time somewhat so that you could leave today. So on behalf of the Bench, I wish you a safe journey home and to -- I would like the usher now to accompany you out of the courtroom. As far as the exhibits are concerned, we shall deal with that tomorrow. We are not going to draw up a list of the exhibits right now. I shall ask the Prosecution tomorrow to give us their exhibits, and I should also ask the Defence to give us a list of exhibits tomorrow also. It is a quarter past 3.00. The court stands adjourned, and we shall resume the hearing again at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.14 p.m.,
